utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, registrar. We are the 19th of March, 2007. Today I would like to greet all the people in the courtroom, the representatives of the Prosecution, the lawyers, the accused. Mr. Coric, I see, is not here today. I hope he will be able to return to the courtroom very shortly. I would also like to greet the court officers the usher. I shall give the floor to the usher so that he can read out two IC numbers for us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you very much Your Honour. OTP has submitted a list of documents to be tendered through Witness L. The list shall be given Exhibit number IC 492. 3D has submitted a list of objections to the document tendered by the OTP through Witness L, and this list shall be assigned Exhibit number IC 493. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, I understood what you said, but I don't think there was a translation of what you said. Just a minute. I'm checking.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I can read again, Your Honours. Okay. OTP has submitted a list of duties to be tendered through Witness L -- no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Still nothing.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter can hear and they are working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't hear anything in any language. I think it should be all right now. Yes, that's fine. Very well. So it's working. The Trial Chamber will hand down an oral decision as far as Petkovic's request of the 12th of March, 2007 is concerned. On the 12th of March, 2007, the Petkovic Defence team sought leave from the Chamber to reply to the Prosecutor's response office, 12th of March -- 7th of measure [as interpreted]-- 2007 concerning its motion dated 12 of February 2007 to take out or withdraw from the indictment allegations of co-perpetration and direct perpetration and direct co-perpetration and complicity. The Trial Chamber feels it should grant Petkovic Defence's request so long as its motion is restricted to issues never addressed before. Consequently, the Trial Chamber rules that Petkovic's Defence has seven days from today onwards to file its reply. Now, as far as the follow-up to Mr. Karnavas's speech on Thursday, a number of things have to be clarified before I take the floor. My colleagues would like to address you and then I shall personally take the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. [In English] On behalf of Judge Trechsel and myself, I wish to make the following statement. Last Thursday, March 15th, 2007, the president of the Chamber, Judge Antonetti sitting on the case of the Prosecution versus Prlic and others made inter alia the following statements: Point 1, and I quote: "And my feeling is, and I've already said that in 90 per cent of the cases, 95 per cent of the cases, most of those questions are in favour of your clients." It is from page -- transcript page 95, lines 2 to 4. According to his ordinance of the President of the same day, he meant to say -- he explained that up to 95 per cent of the questions led to answers favourable to the Defence. Point 2, and I quote again: "So you see, many questions are in favour of the Defence." It is from the transcript page 95, line 13. Then in his ordinance he meant to say that the answers to many questions were favourable to the Defence. Point 3, and I quote from the transcript page 95, lines 13 to 16, and I quote: "And when you say that it is not a totally fair trial, would I like you to tell me of another Chamber that is to such an extent in favour of the Defence." In French, the original, it was said that: "[Interpretation] In favour -- [no interpretation]". We, two of us, we wish to declare that these statements do not reflect our attitude for the following reasons: As far as points 1 and 2 are concerned, we do not keep records of whether answers to our questions may ultimately be considered to benefit one party or the other. We are not aware of any inequality in this respect. As far as point 3, as quoted above, is concerned, we would like to say that while we are certainly mindful of the rights of the Defence, it is our firm belief that the principal task of the Chamber is to ensure that the trial is fair in accordance with Article 20(1) of the Statute. In our view, the pursuit of fairness is tantamount to the search for a balance. [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I shall now take the floor to clarify a number of points, because of course the -- the translation sometimes doesn't always come across as it should, and sometimes don't always reflect what I said. I shall read out what I'm about to say slowly. That last Thursday, on the 15th of March, 2007, Mr. Karnavas took the floor after the testimony of a witness. I responded to him briefly and responded to a number of points. I was unable to give the floor to Mr. Scott, the court officer having told me that due to the recording of the audiotape we could no longer hold the hearing. I shall give the floor today to the Prosecution if it wishes to respond to the comments made in this courtroom. That said, I am taking the floor again today because of a translation problem from French into English which might lead to some confusion or misunderstanding. This is why I wish to shed some light on it. Last Thursday, at the beginning of the afternoon, I came to realise on reading the English transcripts -- transcript, as I did not have the French transcript at that time, that some sentences did not reflect the meaning of what I had said. Therefore, on Thursday afternoon, I immediately informed the parties that I would shed some light on this. I thus rendered an order aimed at providing this clarification and adding a number of sentences in order to add a number of things to my oral conclusion. On reading the French transcript afterwards, I would like to clarify two important points to make quite sure there is no misunderstanding about what I have said. There are two different topics that were briefly addressed last Thursday, the rights of the accused, which is the first topic, and the second, which is a Q and A session. The first pertains to the rights of the accused, i.e., in generic terms, the right of the Defence. The rights of the Defence, as far as I'm concerned, encompass the rights of the accused and the rights of the accused's counsel. It is important to be very clear about this. The rights of the accused means that when an accused person puts a question to the witness as he or she is entitled to do according to the Statute, and the rights of the Defence -- of Defence counsel means, for instance, that Mr. Karnavas can expand on his cross-examination and can do so without being hindered by questions that would upset or interfere with his line of questions. Now, as far as the rights of the Defence are concerned, I have noticed that the transcript in English uses the word "Defence," whereas this means the rights of the accused. So when I say that this Trial Chamber and the Bench have done much for the Defence, I didn't mean in favour of. I just stated that we have done a lot and protect the rights of the Defence. I quoted the Blagojevic case to indicate that this Trial Chamber, pursuant to the Statute, had entitled the accused to put questions directly. To bear in mind the rights of the accused is one thing. To bear in mind the rights of the Defence counsel is another, due to the neutral position of the Judges vis-a-vis the parties. The second topic I'd like to address is the questions and answer process. I think it's important to remember that Mr. Karnavas had asked to hold a hearing to discuss a number of issues he -- or problems he encountered when cross-examining the witness due to questions that had been put by the Bench. This is not the first time that this request was made, and the Trial Chamber felt so far that it was not necessary to hold such a meeting. In light of the assistance of Mr. Karnavas and other counsel and the Prosecutor, we shall in due course hand down a decision on this particular matter. On reading some of the sentences in English in the transcript for somebody who is not well-versed in these matters could lead to some confusion. This is why I feel it is necessary to provide additional -- for additional explanation. When a witness comes to testify, I explain to the witness how this works. I explain to him that there are questions that are going to be put to him. And this is on transcript page 11451, and I shall read out what I said: "The four Judges that are before you, when they deem it necessary, will put questions to you." Let me read it out again: "The four Judges who state before you can, when they deem it necessary, put questions to you." This is in line with the practice and the case law of this Tribunal. The Bench is not restricted to the scope of their question neither in form or content. In addition, you will see that the questions are varying questions. The Prosecution put questions that are not leading. The Defence, as part of the cross-examination, may put leading questions to you. The Bench, therefore, do their utmost to put questions which are as objective as possible, insofar as, on the basis of your answers, we try to understand the situation, or the context, or what it is you're saying. On several occasions in the past I have said to the witness that when a Judge put a question to him or her this question was different in nature to the question put either by the Prosecution or Defence counsel. Each party puts questions to the witness according to the Prosecution's case or Prosecution's -- or Defence case. The Bench wish to discover the truth, and sometimes when they ask their questions this is in line with some of the questions put by either the Prosecution or the Defence. This means that sometimes the Bench wishes to have a more detailed explanation for the answer provided or wishes to put a question on something that has been omitted by either party. Pursuant to Rule 90(F)(i) [as interpreted] of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, the Bench is there to apply the Rules of Procedure and make sure that the truth is unraveled. I have on several occasions specified this, and I have put question after an objection has been raised. You may find this on page 15722 and 15723. I quote: "As a rule, when the Bench asks a question, you will understand that the questions we put are elaborate questions. We pick up on what the witness has said. We add to that what other witnesses have stated, and the question we put is an open question of a general nature which, normally speaking, enables a witness to answer in several ways." Let me give you an example which I mentioned briefly but which is a good indication of what I'm after, what the Bench is after. A while ago a witness answered a question put by the Prosecution, and the same witness talked about the -- the presence of a tank in the Heliodrom, and then the witness had moved on to something else. The Prosecutor had -- hadn't asked any questions to the witness about the presence of this tank in that location either for put the question to the witness, who confirmed that he had seen a tank in the Heliodrom. And if I remember correctly, and I'm quoting: He had even indicated that the tank had fired a shot. A few days later another witness was called to testify it. I waited for the Prosecutor to put questions to the witness about this tank that -- by way of confirming or denying the presence of a tank. The Prosecution did not put the question to the witness. I also waited for Defence counsel to put the question. Defence counsels didn't either. So in the end I put the question to the witness, and I asked him what his view was on the presence of this -- about the presence of this tank. The witness then replied that there was no tank. So, seeking the truth, I put the question to the first witness and then to the second witness. That said, I would like to say that on page 15831 of the transcript I must indicate that there is a mistake there or a slip of the tongue on my part. I would like to quote the sentence in question. "I have already told you in 95 to 90 per cent of the cases the questions we put are in favour of your clients," and I noticed this morning that between the word "question" and "are in favour" I had paused, but being carried away, I had completed my sentence. What I wanted to say was this, and I shall read the sentence out again: "I have already told you that in 95 to 90 per cent of the cases, most of the answers to our questions may be in favour of your clients." This sentence has to be put into perspective and relate to the following pages: 15451 and 15722. This pertains to the questions put by the Bench. If a question is put, this requires an answer. I have said that as far as the end result is concerned, it seemed to me that sometimes several answers had been provided in favour of the Defence. In other cases the answers had been provided in favour of the Prosecution. This might require more scrutiny, but in a number of cases Defence counsel had largely been the beneficiaries of the answers provided to the questions that had been put. My colleagues may not share my point of view, as I have not discussed with them these figures, i.e., 95 to 90 per cent of the cases. The figures might be much lower than the one I have quoted. I have not worked it out personally. This is a feeling I had about it, but I had not checked the figures, the percentage figures. As far as this particular matter is concerned, it is important to indicate that a response provided when a question has been put should be assessed according to its relevance and probative value, and once this answer is provided at a particular point in time the -- the weighing of the answers is, of course, a temporary assessment and in no way can be considered to be a final decision. The final decision only is taken once Prosecution case and Defence case have been heard. The question pur by the Bench, totally unbiased when these questions I put, is part -- these questions are put and comply with the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. The question is there to discover the truth. To achieve this the question may pertain to the credibility of the witness, may pertain to which additional details are required, may pertain to issues not yet raised in the interests of justice. The second point I would like to highlight is as follows: The response provided to a question may, in terms of its provisional assessment and probative value, be either in favour of the Defence case or -- either in favour of the Prosecutor case or in favour of the Defence case. The third point I would like to highlight is the following: The word used in English in the transcript, "Defence," should be understood, according to me, as the rights of the accused. This is what I wanted to say in order to avoid any misunderstanding or misconception. That said, the issue raised by Mr. Karnavas on the holding of a meeting will be decided by the Bench towards the end of the week. Mr. Karnavas's speech last Thursday enabled us to spell things out and better understand the issue which Mr. Karnavas faced. So in the decision I will hand down I hope to meet his demands. Mr. Scott, last time Defence counsel had taken the floor and I had taken the floor, and as we reach the end of the hearing I did not give you the floor. So I would like to give you the floor, if you wish to take it; but if you don't wish to take it, we shall then bring in the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: May it please the Court, I had not intended to speak today for a number of reasons. One is, as usual, we have a very busy trial schedule this week, and even the time we've lost now will impact our ability to complete all the witnesses this week. So it was not my intention to speak this afternoon. Mr. Karnavas last week had asked for time for a hearing to be set in the future, and it was my assessment, if you will, that if in fact the Chamber set such a time that would be the more appropriate time to make any observations that I may have, and I think on Thursday also Judge Trechsel had indicated that it was not the best time to take these matters up because there were only two Judges on the Bench. His Honour Judge Prandler wasn't here, His Honour Judge Mindua wasn't present, so this was not in fact the time to address these matters. So I put that in the context of where we are today. I now feel, however, with the comments that have been made and the Court's, again, intention of setting -- issuing a ruling later this week before the Chamber -- before the Prosecution will have had the opportunity to be heard, that I now feel that if I don't speak now there's no indication that I will have a further opportunity to be heard prior to the time that the Chamber issues a further ruling. Therefore, I feel as if I have no choice, really, but to make my observations at this point. In doing so, I would start by saying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, not to lose time, the decision which the Chamber will hand down will only pertain to the fact whether, yes or no, a hearing will be held on matters relating to the cross-examination and the Prosecution, and whether and how the questions are to be put by the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I hear that and appreciate that, Your Honour, but unfortunately based on past track record, I can't take too much comfort in that assurance. I was about to say a moment ago that unfortunately one of the problems in my respectful submission has developed to date is that Your Honour, Mr. President, you sometimes have a tendency to issue rulings without having heard from the parties and in particular from the Prosecution, and last week the Defence spent about 20 minutes on Thursday without response from the Prosecution. I'm not being critical of the Defence in saying that I'm simply making the observation that the Defence had 20 minutes to address these matters in addition, in addition to any additional time they would receive at a future hearing. The Prosecution up to this moment had received zero minutes. So given the circumstances, Your Honour, I will take my equal amount of time, the 20 minutes, to address the matters that have come before the Chamber. All that is by way of introduction. I now say, may it please the Court, and while I will speak with great respect to the Chamber, the Chamber will also understand if I speak very plainly. A number of people asked me following last Thursday's trial day if I was feeling okay, if I was all right, as I was sitting, you may remember, at the Prosecution bench with my head down. A number of people watching the proceedings asked me about that. I put my head down last Thursday because I was doing the best I could to disappear from this courtroom. I was so embarrassed for this institution, I was embarrassed for myself, I was embarrassed for anyone watching these proceedings. Frankly, I was even embarrassed for the Judges. So I simply wanted to disappear as much as I could. The Prosecution is very concerned whether the victims, the Prosecution, the international community will receive a fair trial in this case. We are very, very concerned about that on a number -- for a number of reasons, including the time limits placed on our case, but also repeated statements and comments by the Chamber and by the President, and the way certain things have been handled. I will keep back to this at the conclusion of my remarks because I want to address specifically some of the points that were raised last week, and I do want to raise without any further risk that the Chamber might issue -- indeed issue a ruling without the Prosecution first having been heard. Party presentation of the case: Mr. President, Your Honour Judge Trechsel, and Your Honour Judge Prandler, I've been practising at this Tribunal for more than nine years. I am well familiar with the oft-made statement that it is a hybrid system and not based on any one national system or any one legal approach. And I certainly agree with that and I deed it has been one of the privileges and pleasures of my experience here over the last nine years to gain greater insights into the other systems, the strengths and weaknesses of various systems, and enrich my own legal experience, my professional experience, having participated in this professional international environment. I am no generic defender or advocate of the adversarial common law system even though I come from that system. Like every system, it has its strengths and its weaknesses. I think there is much that common lawyers can learn from the civil law system. However, I am also no generic defender or advocate of the civil law system. Like every system, it has its strengths and its weaknesses. I think there is much that practitioners from the civil law system can learn from the adversarial common law system. I am also not one who suggests that everything that might be wrong with the ICTY's legal system could be "fixed if only we adopted a civil law system." That is undoubtedly a simplistic position and would not in fact fix, in my view, the various problems or challenges that this institution faces. I see nothing about the civil law system that is inherently superior or more noble than the adversarial system. There are two ways of getting to, hopefully, more or less the same point. Again, they both have their strengths. They both have their weaknesses. Having said all this and when the early Judges and the senior leaders of this institution many years ago designed the system that would be the ICTY, they put in place a system which, hybrid as it is, is decidedly more adversarial than not, decidedly more common law than not. For better or worse, whether the Judges agree with that assessment or the weight given to each system or not, that is the system, that is the path we have gone down these last 13 or 14 years. It is essentially an adversarial system with some adjustments based on the fact, for example, that we have professional Judges and not lay jurors, and because of the nature and circumstances of our cases and evidence, and some of the structural and unique challenges and limitations that this institution faces. Given there, and whether one likes it or not, the adversarial system is primarily a party-driven system. Each party, the Prosecution and the Defence, have both the responsibility, and a weighty responsibilities, and the opportunity to present its case. Not the Court's case, not the Judges' case, its case. The Prosecution case and the Defence case. The Trial Chamber cannot and should not try to perform all roles at once, to be Prosecutor, Defence counsel, Judge, jury and executioner. If the Trial Chamber begins to cast itself in the role of the Prosecution and to shape the Prosecution's case to prove the Prosecution's case against the accused, then I assume that my brethren on the Defence side will object to that. Indeed, I will object to that. Likewise, if the Trial Chamber casts itself as Defence counsel to the accused directing the Defence cases, putting forward and protecting the Defence cases, then indeed I, the Prosecution, will object to that, and presumably, at least in some circumstances, the Defence counsel will object to that. Therefore, as Mr. Karnavas said the other day, the principal role of the Trial Chamber during each party's case is to act as a neutral procedural umpire. To use an American sports example, and I'm sure examples could be drawn from every system, every national sport of those in the courtroom, to use a baseball example you call the because and the strikes, but you don't determine -- you don't tell how -- the batter when to swing and you don't tell the pitcher when to pitch. You do not direct or present the Prosecution's case or the Defence case. Now, specifically on questioning witnesses. In light of what I've just said, a party must be given a reasonable opportunity to conduct its examination according to his or her own plan. A plan is disrupted, it is made more difficult, confusing, takes more time if there are constant interruptions and detours. For example, taking a witness off in a particular direction before the examiner, him or herself, is ready to go in that direction himself or herself. If the Prosecution has not asked a question, Your Honours, or does not ask a question, I would say nine times out of ten there are very good reasons why the Prosecution has not done so. Number one, the Prosecution will indeed ask the question but hasn't gotten to it yet. An examination is not, or should not be, a random -- a series of random questions but is a set of questions hopefully intended and structured to get the evidence before the Chamber. A great time and effort -- a great deal of time and effort, I'm sure not only for the Prosecution but also for the Defence, goes into preparing an examination according to a certain logic and framework. Particular documents may be selected in a particular order for various reasons. Give the examiner an a chance to carry out his or her examination before the Chamber tries to jump ahead and intervene. As I submit to you, Your Honours, I'm pretty confident nine times out of ten, you'll find the examiner is going to get -- was going to get to the same question. Number two, another reason perhaps why the Prosecution either does or does not put a question, the Prosecution has already explored the topic or question in meeting with the witness and already knows essentially what the witness is going to say, that the witness has nothing to say about the topic. Why didn't we ask about, Did you take -- did you walk around the left side of the building to see what was happening on that day? We didn't ask that question because - you know what? - we asked -- we asked that question to the witness when we met with the witness, and the witness said, "I don't know anything about that." Therefore, when we only have very limited amount of time in the courtroom, guess what? We don't ask that question because we know it's not going anywhere. Third, with all respect, the questioner item asked or to be asked by a Judge may be interesting, or to be asked by counsel may be interesting, but again unfortunately either largely irrelevant or less important than other points that have to be pursued, given the time constraints in the case. Your Honours, there is virtually not a single witness that I have presented to the Trial Chamber since this trial started that I would not have asked more or additional questions to or sought to clarify some answer, but we are constantly, every day, faced with the situation of having limited time. I can't ask that question. I skip those questions in my outline. I wish we could clarify that. We don't have time. That is the day-to-day truth that we have to live with. Just to further -- I'm cutting through some of my notes in the interest of time because I think the point's been made. I'll just add this additional item on this point: The same complication happens, Your Honour, when the Prosecution has given the Chamber a good faith estimate of what it thinks the witness -- the time for a witness examination will take. If we say four hours, we didn't just pull that number out of the air. We didn't flip a coin. We didn't role dice. We looked at the evidence, we looked at the statements, and we gave a good -- our best, our good faith based estimate of what we think -- how much time we thought it would take to get the evidence from that witness for the benefit of the Chamber. And when we say four hours, I mean, when I walk in or Mr. Mundis or some other -- one of our other colleagues walks in and says, Well, we decided you have three hours, that has an immediate impact on our ability to present the evidence because now I'm standing on my feet and I'm cutting questions as I go. And indeed, in that environment, I may miss an important question. I may miss an important exhibit, but I'm standing on my feet trying to cut an hour out of an examination based on the limited, shortened time the Chamber has allowed. That is the reality that we have to deal with. I should briefly address the other side of the coin. The Judges may sometimes, Why did the Prosecution spend so much time on that set of questions? And, Your Honour, we may miss -- we may indeed miss it sometimes, but it's because, based on what we know of our overall case - and we do know our case - and maybe some evidence is going to come six months from now, or two weeks from now, how that's going to connect. And something that may seem to you, on first blush, as a waste of time may indeed be, or we wouldn't be offering it, important evidence that we believe the Chamber should hear. Now maybe the Chamber will decide ultimately that it wasn't important, but of course we can't know that. This takes us full circle to my opening point, and that is the Prosecution is presenting the Prosecution's case. It is not presenting the Court's case. It is not presenting any of Your Honours' case. Again, I invite any of Your Honours, if any of you wants to be put on the Defence case, come down and join the Defence; if any of you would like to present the Prosecution case, please come and join the Prosecution. But until that happens, let each of the parties present their case. The Prosecution, Your Honours, as I've told a number of time, are working very, very hard, myself personally and my entire team, to present this case to you as best we can. It won't be perfect. We've made mistakes already; we'll make more mistakes before it's over. But we're working very, very hard to present this case as best we can, under very difficult circumstances I might say. Let us present our case. I turn very quickly to the number and use of exhibits in the case because that was also mentioned last week. The Presiding Judge made comments again about the number of exhibits in the case. First of all, and some of you have heard me say before, there should be no surprise that in a leadership case of this type involving six senior political and military leaders, the six accused in this case, there should be no surprise that this kind of a case would involve a large number, even thousands of documents, just as the Nuremberg trials involved thousands and thousands of documents. In fact, frankly, I'm more bemused when I encounter the reaction in the building, you know, from Judges or from other legal staff, This seems like an awful lot of documents to us. We can't possibly deal with that. And I have to respond to that, the only way I can respond to that, Your Honours, is to say: What kind of cases did people think they were coming to the Tribunal to deal with? These are not second degree burglary cases where someone stole a bicycle and a couple of silver dishes. They are complex, complicated cases, and they require a great deal of evidence, including a great deal of documentary evidence. So no one, no one should be surprised at the nature of the evidence that is required to present one of these cases. This is indeed a -- largely a document case. I'm not sure if the Chamber has fully appreciated that. The Chamber is only going to ever hear a small percentage of the total evidence from the witness. A witness account, the witness who was a victim in a village can only take you so far. But a great deal of this evidence in this case lies in the documents, the internal documents of the HVO and the organisations that these men were part of, and if the Chamber does not receive that documentation by whatever means appropriate, and we can touch on that further if and when we have time, indeed the Prosecution will not have been given an adequate opportunity to present its case, and the Chamber will have not received some of the very most important evidence in the case, because it's in the documents. You have to look at and study the documents. Further, we don't expect the Prosecution to actually tender anything like 10.000 exhibits. Of course not. As we have said before, the trial process is a living, breathing process. The need for particular proof changes and evolves as the trial goes forward. It happened just last week. There were a number examples with the evidence of the witness last week. I won't go into the reasons for them, but Mr. Flynn and I at the end of the day went back and said, We really thought that was going to be disputed but - you know what? - it wasn't. So we don't have to put on any more evidence of that. So we cut evidence. We cut exhibits. It's not disputed. It was admitted in court. The Defence said, That's not an issue. So we adjust our proof. We don't think it will be anything like 10.000 exhibits but it will certainly be thousands, certainly be thousands. And further, Your Honour, it's not the number of exhibits but how they are dealt with. In the Tuta Stela case which I tried, and a much smaller case, crime base, much smaller than this one, two accused at a much lower level than these six men, we put forward -- the Prosecution tendered and had admitted approximately 2.450 Prosecution exhibits in a much smaller case than this one. That case had nothing to do with Stolac or Capljina or any number of places, Gornji Vakuf. It was a much smaller case, 2.450 Prosecution exhibits. The Presiding Judge in that case, Judge Liu, did not seem to encounter any problems with that. They came in, they were handled in good stride, there was no reason -- there is no reason that this Chamber should have any problems with the volume of exhibits, properly managed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, could you give the figures again for the transcript because -- exclamation marks instead. If my colleague had seen it, he would have said so himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. In the Tuta Stela case, the Prosecution tendered and had had admitted 2.450 exhibits and I checked those statistics just over the weekend. In fact, in my nine years at the Tribunal, Your Honours, I have heard it said a number of times, including by Judges, including in the context -- no, I won't say that because I shouldn't probably comment. In a number of contexts "why doesn't most of these exhibits be admitted before the trial starts? Couldn't we save a lot of time if so much of this was handled during the pre-trial process?" I have heard that said repeatedly, including, again, as I say, by ICTY Judges. The evidence in this case could be received more efficiently, or could have been. The Prosecution tried to do, tried to present both through pre-trial motions and earlier particular witnesses to submit collections of exhibits. Indeed at an earlier time, Your Honour, Mr. President, during the pre-trial phase you indicated that a collection of exhibits from a particular organisation or operation, I'll just choose one by example, ECMM, would be admissible through a single representative witness from that organisation. The Prosecution took that to heart. We prepared our case accordingly. Unfortunately, for whatever reason, we then removed away from that to a much more cumbersome regime for the admission of documentary evidence. Now, having said that, I think we may have -- there may be different views on this in the courtroom but I think we've moved in the direction of more efficiency, handling documents and exhibits more efficiently and we have moved, in my submission, in the right direction. I hope that we will continue to do so. I will preview, I will preview to Your Honours and to the Defence that in the next few weeks we anticipate tendering a large -- another large set of documents being largely the HVO documents received from the Croatian government, including the HVO archive in this case. That will indeed be a further -- shall I use the word test, or indication of our ability to present this case in a fair and efficient way. Let me come back, Your Honour, and I'm about to conclude with my more general -- I'm coming back to the more general concerns I stated at the outset. I am very concerned, I am very concerned, Your Honours, as a professional, as someone who is very committed to this process, I'm very concerned that the victims, the Prosecution, and the international community are not going to receive a fair trial in this case. I'm very concerned about that. If one learns by watching what appears to work or what succeeds for others, I think sometimes the Prosecution should be much more vitriolic, should be much more adamant and - how shall I say it? - exercised about our positions. But I would resist doing that, Your Honour, because I would hope that the Chamber ultimately - ultimately - will respond more to reason and common sense than to vitriolic statement. I know that the Chamber has comment -- has made its comments today which we take on board, but I have to say again that what I heard last Thursday, and frankly what most of the English speaking world heard, and I heard this from outside this -- the ICTY, I heard it from outside the OTP, was great concern at what had been said when the statement, to this effect, and again so there's no misunderstanding, now corrected, but the statement that was heard on Thursday, I dare say around the world, was this one: "And my feeling is, and I've already said, that in 90 per cent of the cases, 95 per cent of the cases most of those questions are in favour of your clients. So you see, many questions are in favour of the Defence. And when you say that it is not a totally fair trial, I would like to -- I would like you to tell me of another Chamber that to such an extent in favour is in favour of the Defence."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, I have provided a corrigendum. You talk about Thursday, and I have corrected the meaning of that sentence. So if you have prepared what you are saying now beforehand, I understand. Maybe you did not understand what I said a while ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I have understood, Your Honour, the corrections, and I'm just simply telling you where many of us were coming from and reacting to last Thursday based on what we heard -- what was heard in the courtroom, and I know what -- and what other people heard. I state my concerns about the fairness of the trial. I won't state it -- I'll leave it to the Defence, of course, to state their positions, as they always have in a forceful way. I hope the Trial Chamber will prove me wrong, and that is when I say prove me wrong, my concerns about the fairness of the trial to the victims, to the Prosecution itself, and to the international community. But I have to say to Your Honours to speak plainly, and other counsel have gotten away with speaking plainly so please extend to me the same opportunity, I'm not persuaded simply by words. Words, unfortunately, are easy to deal with. They can be explained away as translation errors or misunderstanding or what have you. Actions speak louder than words, and it is the actions, not just the words, of the Chamber that I and my colleagues will be watching. I take my responsibility, Your Honours, for those of you have not noticed, to the victims and to the international community, indeed to what I consider the extremely important Prosecution function itself very seriously. I have said it before. I will say it again. The victims and the Prosecution and the international community are absolutely just as entitled to a fair trial as the accused. Not more of a fair trial but also not less of a fair trial. Not something of a fair trial, not sort of a fair trial, but a fair trial. And just as Mr. Karnavas and some of the other Defence counsel may get very agitated and noisy at times about fairness to the Defence, Your Honour, I'm going to be, if necessary, and if that's what it takes - if that's what it takes - I will be just as agitated and noisy about fairness to the Prosecution. With respect, with great respect to all three of you and also to Judge Mindua, who is absent, if you think that I, as a Prosecutor, am going to sit back and watch a double standard being applied of fairness and different treatment for the Defence, even now in the Defence case when the Prosecution has been treated differently on the feeling or kind of expressing an opinion or an attitude of, well, it's only the Prosecution, we can give it less concern, less concern for fairness. We can tell the OTP what to do; it's only the OTP, after all. But I am afraid, Your Honours, if that's the Chamber's -- ever the Chamber's attitude you have the wrong Prosecutor. You have the wrong Prosecutor. Because whatever other Prosecutors might do, I will not sit back and allow that to happen without comment. And I close with this: As I said, I do not mean -- I hoped not to make these comments this afternoon but I felt at the end that I really had to. I've often wondered what it would be like if we had six victims sitting behind the Prosecution side over here. Six victims to whom the Chamber would say hello to everyday. Six victims who could ask questions of witnesses. Six victims who could pop up at any moment and make comments and arguments and statements to the Chamber. Six victims who could express their views on whether they, and the thousands of people like them, believe that they are receiving a fair trial. I will be firm, Your Honour, about representing those victims and representing our interest. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, I shall give you the floor. Mr. Scott, we've listened to you. As I have told you, we will hand down a decision and try to meet the legitimate demands of each party. So await the decision before making any final pronouncements. We have not handed down a decision yet. We know why Mr. Karnavas said he wanted to cross-examine without being interrupted, and he clearly told us why. You have also explained quite a number of things to us right now, and I am sure that this decision will bear in mind the interests of both parties. Mr. Karnavas, please do not -- please do not -- sorry, add any water to the pan and make it short.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll be very brief. First I want to commend the Prosecution for its comments, and I, for one, at least have tried to express the same sentiments with respect to the right of the Prosecution to put on its case and to represent the rights of the victims. Number two, I ask for the hearing, and that's what I wanted to say, that before a decision is made, I think we do need a hearing. You have an unprecedented situation here where both the Defence and the Prosecution are, at least in my opinion, or unlike my experience in 25 years, both are crying for a fairer process, and they both seem to be joined in that -- in that request. The Prosecution moved for certification, this is now the second time, on the reasoning as to why their time was cut. We joined in that certification process, we the Defence, on the basis that the Trial Chamber did not give sufficient reasoning at the request of the Appeals Chamber, based on the remand. We do think a hearing should be held as expeditiously as possible. This is not something that is going to go away. I'm not as eloquent as Mr. Scott or some of my other colleagues, but I must say, if we could just have a hearing where we could just clear out some of these technical issues, I think that would -- the case can proceed. This is by far -- when you look at the indictment and when you look at the size of the case, this is by far the most complex case that exists today and that will exist for the remainder of this Tribunal, and I think your colleagues will understand if it's going to take us a little bit longer. And so I think that we have tried to make the process smoother, faster, more efficient, but I think now we probably need to take a step back and see how we can get the train back on the tracks. It's not too late. But in any event, I just want to remind Your Honours that we would like to have this hearing, and again I want to thank Mr. Scott for his eloquence today. I share in the Prosecution's pain in trying to get their case. There's nothing more frustrating than an advocate who has worked very, very hard and is unable to put on their narrative for their questions as a result of some interruptions. The results may be unintended, but nonetheless when you're on this side of the table it can be rather frustrating. And again I want to apologise for having raised my voice last week. It was clearly not intended as disrespectful but I've been cursed with this personality. I'm going to work on it some more, to be much more understanding to -- to your interventions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karnavas. I have asked for the floor. The President has given it to me. I recall what I have said. It was an exchange between yourself and myself on Thursday, that the hearing you have asked the Chamber to decide upon, you have practically started it on Thursday. I -- I would have hoped that we would have had it perhaps in a -- in a reduced composition, in the absence of the accused, because it's a matter of pure legal issues. I can very well understand, Mr. Scott, that you felt you wanted to put your nail into the board, too, as the other party has it. I'm aware of the fact that some other Defence counsel also would like to intervene in this more thoroughly, but still I think we should not do it surreptitiously but should now go to the hearing of the witness who is waiting. It's also a matter of politeness, not to let them wait for hours. So perhaps the President will decree the break right now and then we can settle down to work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, you are on your feet. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. As Mr. Scott, the representative of the OTP, presented certain views which have to do with us accused here, as well and everybody else, and that is in view of the fact that victims exist and the accused are already here sitting here in the courtroom that the equation -- simple equation, according to Mr. Scott, is that we have already been convicted and that Their Honours need not, say, give us the time of day and say hello. This goes against the rights of Europe. We are innocent until proved guilty, until there's a court ruling about our guilt. Now, as regards the international community on the victims, the victims of what happened in the former Yugoslavia, we know what happened in the former Yugoslavia. We know all the things that happened. And as to the concept of the international community, it has not yet been defined and there are 500 to 600 wars which the international community among other things and among others the country from which Mr. Scott comes from waged after World War II. We don't remember any trials being held, but there were if not -- there were just as many victims in as there were in the former Yugoslavia if not more. Now, after the French Revolution, in Europe a principle was heralded by which everybody was equal before the law --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak. Mr. Praljak, you have been given a right to ask questions because sometimes the accused can know better than his lawyer what the facts were, but you are not here as a lawyer, and I should not intervene on a question like this. Your counsel can do that. Thank you. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I think that according to the Statute I do have the right to present views which are opposed to other people's views, Judge Trechsel. Please. He directly went along these lines and I want to ask one more thing. It has to do with elements -- we're talking about a fair trial and rights. Now, I would like to say the law according to which Mr. Scott wishes accuse and then ask that I be found guilty do not hold true for Mr. Scott, and the justness of a thesis like that is something that we could debate. And if we are debating it, then I, as an intellectual, regardless of how far I've been trained in the law, do have the right to say what I want to say, because Mr. Scott is trying me under the laws that do not apply to him. I have just as many -- just as much right here as anybody. Thank you for your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Mr. Praljak. It is now 3.30. We shall bring in the witness. Mr. Scott, are there protective measures for the upcoming witness? I believe not. No. No protective measures. You have planned to lead this witness for an hour and a half and the Defence will have an hour and a half, so we shall have a 20-minute break now and resume in 20 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Before Mr. Karnavas took the floor, Judge Antonetti said: "You needn't add fuel to the fire to make matters worse as everybody is calm today."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, I think we need an IC number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 4D has submitted a list of objections to document tendered by the OTP through Witness DE. Such list shall be given Exhibit number IC 494. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. I hope you hear the translation in your mother tongue. Could you give us your first name, family name, and date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Salem Cerenic, and I was born on the 16th of October, 1962, in Vares.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Do you have an occupation? Are you employed currently?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what you mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you employed? Do you work? What do you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I work in the Vares municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Sir, have you already testified before a court in the events that unfolded in your country, or is it the first time that you come to testify today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I testified at the cantonal court in Zenica, also linked to the case of Vares-Stupni Do, the events dating back to 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I would like you to take the oath, please, and read what's on that sheet of paper.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, just some explanation I'd like to give you. You are a Prosecution witness. A number of questions will be put to you by Mr. Flynn whom you have met I believe yesterday or this morning. The Prosecution will have an hour and a half to ask you questions, after which Defence counsel and sometimes the accused will put questions to you as part of the cross-examination. The Bench, which faces you, can also put questions to you if it so deems it is necessary. That said, questions put are neither in favour of the Prosecution, neither in favour of the Defence, are just put with a view to discover the truth. I will only put questions to you once Prosecution has finished and once the Defence counsel has finished, which will enable me to check out the translation at the same time. So I shall now give the floor to Mr. Flynn.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good afternoon to Your Honours; good afternoon members to Defence and everybody else in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And good afternoon, Mr. Cerenic. I believe you're from the town of Vares. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's where I was born too.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And can you tell it us where you were living in the first half of 1993?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: I've already said that from birth I've been living in Vares, and at the time, that is in 1993, I lived there with my family, my wife, and my two children. We lived in Vares.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And at that time did you have an occupation, or how did you occupy yourself?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: In 1993, I was a member of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: When did you join the BH army?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: I joined at the beginning of 1993, straight away in January.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Can you tell us which unit you were a member of, what your rank was, and what your duties were, please?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: I didn't have a rank of any kind, but I was member of the platoon attached to the staff in Vares municipality and performed the task of a security detail. I provided security for facilities, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And were you stationed in Vares all of -- all during 1993?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Can you tell us where else you were stationed and why you moved to there?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: If I understand the question correctly, I was at the battlefront for a time facing the Chetniks, mostly. And in the unit attached to the staff, as I said, I provided security for individual facilities and buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Have you ever heard at the time of a town or village called Dabravine?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Were you ever attached to any unit there?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: You mean in Dabravine?

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: In Dabravine I was a member of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And why did you move from Vares to Dabravine?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: It wasn't only me who was moved. On the 1st of July, 1992, the HVO units forcibly took power from the legally elected authorities in Vares so that the HVO was in Vares, and all the other legally elected authorities, like the police, the War Presidency of the municipality, was moved to Dabravine.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: So moving to the summer of 1993, you were in Dabravine on the front line; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did something happen to you when you were on the front line?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: I was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And what injuries did you sustain?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: I was wounded by the shells in my right leg and my shoulder, shoulder blade.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did you have to spend some time in hospital?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was in hospital, but I can't remember for how long. I was put up in Breza, which was the clinic at the time. We couldn't enter Vares to receive treatment at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, you were in Dabravine during this period. Did you get leave from your unit from time to time to visit your family?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: I think it was in September that I requested leave from my superiors. I asked them to let me go for two reasons. At that time, my late mother was very ill, and I asked to go and visit her. And the second reason was that I had to go home because we didn't have any money to buy firewood for heating during the winter. So I went into the forest to cut down some firewood and take it home. So those were the reasons for which I requested a little longer leave of absence.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And during the month of October where did -- the early part of the month of October leading up to the middle of October, where were you?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: I was in Vares.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, do you remember at some stage during the month of October, while you were in Vares, did you receive news concerning visitors arriving to the town?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: On the 21st and 22nd, I think -- well, I don't know the exact date, but a neighbour of mine came by with his wife, and he told me that about 200 Ustasha soldiers had arrived in Vares led by their commander, Ivica Rajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: When you say Ustasha soldiers, did he -- did he describe the name of the unit? Did he identify the units that had arrived, the soldiers who -- which had arrived?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Well, I think he mentioned the Apostoli and the Maturice. They were units from Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: At that time in October of 1993 did you know anything about the units, Apostoli or Maturice?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: I had heard of them through the local television station, and when they took over power in Vares they had installed -- or, rather, the local television station was operational. It was called Bobovac of the Vares Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: In Vares town itself, did Vares have its own military unit?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: There were only the HVO units in town, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Was that unit known as the Bobovac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it was called.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, referring to these it troops who had come from Kiseljak, did you know at the time why they had arrived to Vares?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Well, no. We weren't informed that they had arrived, let alone the reason for their arrival. But at that time Bosnia was well-known that other units -- when other units went to another town there would be trouble there. And when we used the word "belaj" meaning "trouble" in Bosnia, it meant that they would do something bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did the arrival of these units cause you any concern or were you relaxed about it?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that in my last answer I answered this question too. It caused an upset. The population became upset when units came in from outside somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did anything unusual occur to your family immediately after their arrival?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: On the 23rd, in the morning, straight away, three people in camouflage -- when I say camouflage, they were wearing camouflage uniforms and had soot on their faces. They had some sort of -- well, I'll call it soot, but their faces were covered in black. They stormed into my house where my wife, my two children, and I myself were sitting.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of these soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And were you able to determine from their uniforms which military force they represented? Did you recognise the uniforms?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Yes. On their sleeves, I don't know whether it was the left or right sleeve, but they had the HVO insignia, HVO patches on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: But you didn't recognise any of them. At that time, would you have known -- as -- as a resident of Vares at that time, would you have known soldiers who made up the HVO Bobovac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: I knew most of them, but Vares is a very small town and everybody knows everybody else. So had I known any of them -- well, no, I didn't know them. They were from elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: So can you describe for the panel, please, what happened after they came into your house?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Three men stormed into the house, three soldiers wear camouflage uniforms whom I didn't know, and they started shouting. They said, "Give us your money, your weapons, and your gold." Of course I didn't have any weapons or gold or money, so I had nothing to give them basically. There was a lot of provocation. They swore a lot. They called us "balija" and, "You Turk," and words of abuse like that. They cursed my mother, father. And the more they insisted, at one point they shoved a rifle into my mouth, asked for what I told you earlier on, money, gold or weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: So are we to understand that you didn't give them any money at all?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember exactly whether I gave them anything. I can't quite remember. If I had some on -- if I had some, I would have given them some.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: So after making these demands, what then happened? Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Well, to put it mildly, they threw me out of my own house without letting me put anything on to keep me warm. It was October. It was cold. They didn't let me put anything on my feet, and I think I was just wearing a T-shirt of some sort. A red one it was, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: So you weren't dressed in your ABiH uniform at the time they came to your house? You were in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And while you were outside the house, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: They pushed me and shoved me with their small arms. They threw me out of my house and out of my yard. And there were some small groups, so I might have seen about 50 or 70 metres from the house another little group of soldiers, and they ordered me to run towards them with my head down looking at the ground, not to look left or right, and I had to keep my hands behind -- hold my hands behind my head. And I went from one group to the other. They shouted at me, swore at me. Well, I suppose you want me to repeat all this. I heard coming from the side, so I suppose they were expelling other people, too, because I could hear this same sort of shouting a little ways away. So that's how we left, with these swear words being shouted at us. And we were taken to in front of the secondary school building or centre, which was called Ivan Goran Kovacic in Vares, and they took us inside and took us to the gymnasium hall of this secondary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Before you were forced to proceed off to this secondary school, do you remember, were you wearing a wedding ring?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: A wedding ring. The wedding band as we call it. That's what you get when you marry. Yes, I did have a wedding ring on my finger, and at Vratnica, the exit to -- when I was going outside my yard, one of these Ustashas said, "Take that off your hand, your finger." I said that was my wedding ring and he shouted out that I should take it off, so I did take it off or he'd cut off my finger. So I did take it off and I gave it to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Okay. So going back you were forced to go towards Goran -- this Ivan Goran Kovacic. How far would that have been from your house that you were forced to run in your bare feet? Or without shoes, I should say.

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Well, it's not a straight road. It curves for about a kilometre. Perhaps a bit more than one kilometre. Not less. I would say more, but thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And what happened witness you got to the school?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: When we reached the school, as I said, they forced us inside to the sports hall of that same secondary school. So I entered the school, and I saw -- well, there were already some 70 to 100 other people there in the sports hall. The only thing that was evident was that a man was lying down in the middle of the hall, and let me say that the town is a very small one, so we all knew each other mostly, but I managed to find a seat, somewhere to sit down amongst all those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And this man lying down in the sports hall, did you know him?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Can you describe him and name him for us, if you do?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Ibro Likic. He was wearing a light blue uniform, the kind that the civilian protection wore at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And was there anybody with this man or was he alone?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: As I said, he was lying down on the floor, and there were two uniformed people, two uniformed men standing above him. Well, I don't know when there were two, but I think two.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And do you know what he was doing lying on the floor? Did you hear any words spoken to this man?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Well, the men standing above him, the soldiers, shouted at him. Well, I don't have to mention that they kept swearing at them. They called them balijas, Turks, and so on, and they asked for -- where his hunting rifle was because he was a hunter at the time quite legally. So he -- they told him to surrender his hunting rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Can you remember what condition this man was in?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: He was in a very bad state physically. He was all bashed about on his face. He was bleeding. He had bruises. He was all black and blue, and quite visibly he'd been beaten up a great deal.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And what age would this man have been at that time approximately?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if I can give you an approximation, but he was over 40, thereabouts. Yes, he was certainly over 40.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity of looking around the hall, and did you recognise any of the other 70 to a hundred people that you said were in the hall when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: The persons who were present in the room, of course, yes, in the hall, I saw them all. They were people from Vares. I repeat yet again that we all know each other because it's a small town. I knew everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And can you tell us were there any females amongst these people?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And from what ethnic division would these people have come from?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: They were all Bosniaks, Muslims, who were forcibly brought into the hall. They were Bosniak Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Were you in a position to see whether they were young or old or middle-aged? What ages would these people have been?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: All ages, all ages, say from age 16 up to 70. Very old men, grandfathers.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Were you told why you had been brought there to the -- to the school and what was going to happen to you by anyone?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: No one said anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And so, when you told us that there were 70 to a hundred people when you arrived initially. Did these numbers stay static or were some of them released, or did the numbers increase?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: No, no. The number increased from one minute to the other, unfortunately. Of course they were all Bosniaks, Muslims, who were brought there forcibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: So how many people do you say were held in the school at the end of the day on the 23rd of October, 1993? How many people were in this hall or gym?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Well, around 300 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And were you given any instructions by anybody to -- on what to do while you were in there, inside the building?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: They were giving us instructions, HVO soldiers were. They were telling us that we put everything we had in front of us, everything, everything we had in our pockets. Somebody had, say, rings, jewellery, keys. Whatever they had on them or in their pockets. Quite simply we were forced to take everything off and out and put it in front of us, and then they would come up and take all of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Do you remember on this first day if the HVO approached you for anything else apart from taking these things from you, as you've just described?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: You're asking me personally?

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes. Did anybody person -- did any of these soldiers personally approach you at any stage on this first day?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: The first day, yes. One of these men in uniform spoke to me. He walked in through the door and said, "Who is Salem Cerenic?" I was really, really surprised to hear that, because I didn't really know any of these soldiers and I was wondering how it was that they knew me, and he asked me to come up to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And what happened then?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: When he call out my first and last name he told me to come up to him. I was sitting closer to the end of that gym, and I came up to him. I was a few metres away from him only, and he ran into me, jumped at me, kicked me in the chest, and I fell on the ground. While I was on the ground, others had joined him. He was not on his own. He did not enter the hall on his own. There were five or six of them, I think, who entered the hall, and they all started beating me with whatever they had in their hands. They had bats. They had rifle butts. They were kicking me with their feet, and they had these heavy boots on their feet. So they were hitting me, kicking me. That's when they started, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And as they were beating you as you've described, or even after, did they give any explanation for this treatment?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Well, first they asked who Salem Cerenic was, or in actual fact they called out my name, and it seemed to me that later they called me Kiseljacanin, as in man from Kiseljak. They had received some kind of information that I was on the front, around Kiseljak, as a member of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And again, all of this was accompanied with cursing of my balija mother, Turkish mother, how come they hadn't killed me there, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And how long did this beating last for?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: The first one?

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes, this beating that you're talking about now.

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it went on for almost an hour, because the seven of them were taking turns, actually. So they would bounce me from one to the other. I don't know. And then if one of them would get tired then the other one would take over, and it went on that way for almost an hour. On that occasion they kicked out two of my teeth. They broke my ribs and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did you sustain any other injuries apart from broken teeth, broken ribs?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. There were visible injuries on my face. I had haematoma on my face. I was black and blue. You can imagine what it looks like if a man is beaten by six or seven other men with I don't know what. I already told you bats, rifle butts, hands, legs, not to go into all of that again.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Please remember that the Judges don't know any of this now. You're addressing them and you're telling the story to them. I know you and I have talked about this before, but the Judges haven't heard your story before. Did you -- while they were beating you, did you receive any blows to the head?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Blows to the head? Of course. And X-rays established afterwards that -- now, I can't remember how doctors called this. My skull was fractured in a few places, and I'm suffering from the effects of that to this day. I have terrible headaches, and also my cervical spine has been in bad shape to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Well, immediately after the beating, do you remember were you conscious?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say with any degree of certainty as to how conscious I was, but I think that I remember, well if I can put it that way, that I crawled on all fours to the place where it was that I was supposed to be sitting. This beating took place in the hall, and I crawled on all fours or perhaps a colleague helped me to get back to the wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And can you tell us, were you the only one singled out to be beaten on this first day?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Well, I've already mentioned Ibro Likic who was lying right in the middle of the hall all black and blue, visibly beaten up. They were calling out peoples names. There were three or four men who were Albanians and who were called out. They said, "The Siptars should come out." And I saw that they were beaten up indeed. And this man called Adanalic who still lives in Vares, of course, and then I and Ibro Likic, and then you could hear the beating. I mean, you could hear beatings in addition to the ones I've already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did you know any of the persons carrying out these beatings?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Were you offered any kind of medical assistance after the beatings for the injuries that you sustained, or did you ask for any medical assistance?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: I didn't get anything as for medical assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: How long were you kept in the gym, in high school? How many days were you kept in it?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: I personally? I personally was there for five or is six days, I think. I personally and a group of other people. And then they carried out some kind of selection. I don't know. Say, they singled out about half of the military-aged men to the hall of the Vladimir Nazor school in Vares. And in this gym the people who stayed behind were very old and sickly, whereas we military-aged men were transferred to Vladimir Nazor. That's what the school was called then, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately how many men went to the second school, the Nazor school, and how many people were left behind in the original high school?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Well, more than half of us were taken or transferred to this elementary school. If you want to talk in terms it of numbers, perhaps 160 or 170 of us were transferred to the elementary school and the rest stayed at the secondary school in the hall there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Before we move to the secondary -- the second school that you're talking about to where you were moved after five to six days, can you just briefly tell us during the five to six days you were kept in the high school the conditions that were existing in the high school, can you tell us if you received food? Did you have water? Did you have water to wash, to drink? Did you have water to wash? Did you have toilet facilities?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: None of that. We had none of that. We had -- well, if I can put it this way: If they were in a good mood they would let us leave for about 10 seconds to relieve ourselves. As for food, I think that the first day or two, people coming from the municipal Red Cross would bring us food, but then they did away with that as well. We lay on gym mats. You know what gym mats are? How could I explain this? Those are things that you have in a gym. I don't know if I can explain that. So not everybody was lucky enough to be lying on a gym mat. Some had to lie and sleep on the floor, the parquet floor, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: This was October, mid-October. What were the weather conditions like inside the hall? I mean, was it cold, warm?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Vares is cold, a cold town generally speaking even in the month of August, and in October it was cold indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: So turning now the to second school to where you were brought. Can you tell us what happened to you when you were there? First of all, can you tell us were you beaten in this school?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, they beat us there too. I have to say with a lesser intensity, if I can put it that way. Not as often as over there. If I were beaten, say, five or six times, if I went through this torture five or six times out there, then here it was two or three times a day. So they reduced it bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And how long were you kept in this second school?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
