utterances.text: In the second school, I don't know exactly how much time we spent there, because we were actually taken to two or three different locations within that school, within the building itself. We were at two or three different locations or, rather, we were hidden in two or three different locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And can you tell us why you were hidden? What was the purpose of your being hidden in these two or three different locations?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Well, we talked about it amongst ourselves, and it seemed to us that the main reason was that we should not be seen. The International Red Cross came to register the camp inmates, and since we were - how should I put this? - group of 25 or 27 men, and we were beaten up very visibly, so they were hiding us so that the representatives of the International Red Cross would not see us. Also, they said that it was UNPROFOR that was coming there at the time, that they were coming to see the inmates.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And this group of people who were beating up, you said it was quite visible. Can you tell us what age group of men this was? Were they the same age as you or older, younger?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Well, at any rate all of us were military-aged men, say from 20 to 35 up to 40.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And you told us about being beaten in the second location again. Not as severely as you had been -- or as frequent as you had been in the previous -- in the first location. Did you sustain any additional injuries in this second location from these beatings?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: They only made things worse. They only made the injuries that I had already sustained even worse. I told you that I had many broken ribs and teeth knocked out and fractured bones perhaps. So -- well, we in Bosnia would say that I was like a broken wickerware basket.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And I asked you about the first school, the conditions, and asked you to describe them. Can you tell us were the living conditions in the second location where you were kept any better? Can you describe the conditions there? Were you given food, water? Did you have facilities -- toilet facilities? Did you have bedding to sleep on? This is the second location, the Nazor school.

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: No, nothing. The conditions hadn't changed over there either.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Well, did you receive any food at any stage during the period you were held there?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And how about the toilet facilities? Were you permitted to go to the bathroom?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: I personally do not remember ever having gone out. As for this school Vladimir Nazor, as for myself and this group of 27 men that I've already referred to, and I've already mentioned that we were taking them -- taking us here or there, from one place to another, I don't remember going to the toilet. I don't remember receiving anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: How about bedding -- were you provided with mattresses there and blankets?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: No way. No, no, no. No. What mattresses? Come on. We didn't even have any blankets.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: So how long in all did you spend in this second school?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: The elementary school, in the gym there? I think I spent two days there. And then from that hall they rushed us out with a lot of swearing to the third floor of that school. They took us to a classroom up there. I cannot remember now how much time I spent there. I know I spent one night there. I'm sure about that, but I'm not sure whether I spent two nights there. And then as for this classroom that we were in, well, you know what a classroom looks like in a school? There is desks and chairs, and we spent the night there. And that is how we spent our time there. And then they rushed us out of there. All of this was done in a great hurry. They took us to the heating room of this same elementary school, and then -- now, I can't remember exactly how much time we spent there, how much time we spent in the heating room, but from the heating room we were taken out of some back door, taken out of that school, and that is when we got out. The Catholic church is right next door to the school, so -- how should I put this? - we were right in the church yard. And actually, they were herding us to the school, or to the church. And then there were these vehicles there and --

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Do you remember the date on which this occurred that you were herded out of the elementary school into the church premises?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: The date? I cannot remember. Well, let me try to do my math and give you an approximation. If I spent five or six days at the school and then -- then another two days in the elementary school, and then -- well, if you put all of it together it's about ten days, nine days or ten days.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Nine days in custody -- in detention before you were moved to the church premises?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: We were not located in the church. That's just the route we took. We were brought to the entrance into the church. We were in the church yard, and there were two vehicles, a small TAM truck and a kombi, I think, and then they herded us onto these vehicles, and then from there they transferred us to a third or fourth or fifth location, whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did this occur during the daytime or at night-time?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Night-time. It happened at night-time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And this -- this third location to where you were taken, can you tell us where this was, what it was?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: They took us in those vehicles to Majdan. Of course we didn't know where we were until we actually get there. Vares-Majdan is a suburb of the town of Vares. It is three kilometres away from Vares. They brought us to a building. We were in front of this old building. Before it was called the so-called old industrial school, and in the basement of that school, well, that's where we were put up. And what was prepared there was kind of prison -- or, rather, there were these rooms or should I call them cells.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And in total how many of you were in put in these rooms or cells?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Well, there were this group that had been taken out to the third floor. There were between 25 and 27 of us. 27, I think, would be more likely.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Were there any other prisoners in this third location when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Were there any guards in the building when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did you know any of them?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: The military police were there. I did know some of the guards. They were members of the HVO of the Vares brigade Bobovac, and I think that I saw some members of their military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And what happened while you were kept there?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: As I was saying, we were in these two cells. We were divided into these two cells. Half were in one and half were in the other. And from there we were taken out to dig trenches. Some people were. Well, most people were -- or, rather, I never went to dig trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Were you beaten while you were in this third location?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Not there. That's where the local people were, if I can put it that way, the local members of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: While you were there did you have any visitors?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Do you mean acquaintances, friends, family members?

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Well, let me put it this way: What -- during the period you were held in this facility did anybody come in and speak to you or did anybody come in and visit you? I don't mean acquaintances or friends.

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: As for friends and acquaintances and family members, they didn't let any of them come. As a matter of fact, they didn't even know where it was that we were. I remember on one occasion soldiers came, and they wore caps, and they had Chetnik cockades on their caps. So there were Chetniks there. They would come there -- rather, they came once.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And did they speak to you when they came?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. One of them, as a matter of fact, said something very taunting or insulting or inhumane. I don't know how to put it. He told us that Stupni Do had been levelled to the ground. I can't remember the exact word he used, but he did mention that Stupni Do had been destroyed and the population killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: At this time, which was October 1993, do you know if there was any cooperation between the Serbs and the Bosnian Croats in the conflict with -- between ABiH and the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Well, specifically in the Vares area the cooperation between the Croatian Defence Council and the Serb territories -- well, the Croats -- or, rather, Vares was surrounded on all sides. On the one side by Serb forces, on the other side by the BH army forces. Now, how they came by this agreement, well, they had their corridor whereby they were able to pass through Serb territory and go down to Croatia. Convoys, they had convoys to bring in food and so on and everything that was necessary for the life of the population in a town.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: So how long did you spend in this third location?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Three or four days, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And what happened after three to four days?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: I know that this cell of ours was right by the road. The wall was right by the wall -- the road, and we had a barred window. We weren't able to see through it very well, through the window, but we heard Croatian soldiers with megaphones, with loudspeakers, going out and appealing to the Croatian population to evacuate from the lower part of Vares, called Vares-Majdan, to Vares, and then from Vares through Serb territories that I mentioned a moment ago onwards to Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Were you released from this detention centre?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: No, no. We managed to escape on our own. We broke down the door and fled.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And after fleeing, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: When we broke through the entrance door and broke out through the cell, at the entrance door itself there was an iron door there. We found a key there, but all the HVO guards had escaped and gone to see what was happening to their families. We found the key and managed to go out onto the road, and at one point we saw UNPROFOR, an APC belonging to UNPROFOR, and we waved to them and gesticulated and used sign language, and they took us in. And they called in two or three other APCs, and they transported us to Vares that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And was this the end of your ordeal in detention?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: When I reached the Vladimir Nazor elementary school in Vares, I came across the population from Vares there. There were some people there, and the school was guarded by UNPROFOR soldiers and I felt very safe there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, were you able to return to your regular duties with your ABiH unit immediately after securing your release?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: No, no. I couldn't do that, and I mentioned a moment ago that I was so badly beaten up, with so many fractures that I spent several months undergoing treatment, and afterwards I didn't return. And they helped me out and offered me a job, and in fact it's the job that I still do today.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And was this treatment arranged through the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat that question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: The treatment that you got for your injuries, was that arranged through the ABiH or did you arrange it independently?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: It was in the local health centre in Vares. That's where I was treated by a doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I wonder with the assistance of the usher if the witness could be shown the booklet of exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And Mr. Cerenic, I'd like you to turn to the first exhibit number, 06042. And it's in English and in Bosnian. You'll need to turn about eight to nine pages until you come to the Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, do we need to spend time on showing this document, because the document -- well, we cannot speak of the authenticity of the document. It hasn't got a stamp or a signature or a number or when it was compiled or who it was compiled by or anything like that, and also the medical documents attached to the document, at least in certain parts of it, not in all of it, but we can't see that there were any injuries that could be linked to the torture the witness allegedly suffered, because one of them just speaks about an eye examination, no trauma. In another case, again there's a borderline syndrome mentioned which according to my modest knowledge has nothing to do with that. It's a psychological state that could have existed earlier. But anyway, my objection is raised on the fact that it would be difficult to ascertain the authenticity of the document. It hasn't got the elements necessary for being admitted into evidence. It hasn't got any of the different elements. I don't mind setting aside the medical documents from -- of this witness. He can say if he recognises them, that's fine, but as to the rest, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Flynn, I think you're going to answer this. Could you reply to the objections -- to the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honours. I do appreciate that -- that there are no -- that there are no signatures on some of the documents, but if I can direct Your Honours to the Bosnian documents at the start of the Bosnian package. You will see that there appear to be photocopies of stamps. The document, I can tell you, for what it's worth at this stage, the document was presented to us by the Bosnian authorities, and I was merely going to ask the witness some short questions to see whether or not the findings of the various specialists mentioned in the medical reports were consistent with the injuries that he had described to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall turn to my colleagues and ask them what they think about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as I said, I don't object to the witness dealing with the medical documents where his name is mentioned, but now I'm talking about the technical aspect. These documents were offered along with one other document as a part of that document, and we don't know anything about that basic first document, who, when, how, or anything like that. So if the Prosecution wishes to use the medical documents referring to this witness, because there are others that don't have anything to do with the witness, they can go ahead. We don't object to that. And quite obviously the witness can say, "Yes. I went to see doctor that day and that is what it says." But he can't claim that or state anything about the other witnesses, and he cannot address the document itself, nor can anybody confirm what the document in fact is, because on page 2 we can see an index, the contents of the document. So it is obviously a part of something else, a part of some other document, but we have no way of checking that out. So that's an unknown quantity. And then on page 3 we see a description of the event but we don't see who, when, what or anything like that. And then page 4 we see that this is an attachment, these medical documents are an attachment. So we can deal with the attachment through this witness and as far as he is concern, but not as far as anybody else is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Flynn, on looking at the document, the first page is a three-line summary. The second page is a table of contents, description of events, medical documentation, 19 pages, a Red Cross identification, 37 pages, statements of detained person, 418 pages. I don't have the 37 pages relating to the identification process, and I don't know where this document comings from. Could you shed some light on this for us, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: All I am in a position to do think stage, Your Honour, and this was one of the documents that I would be presenting obviously as an exhibit, all I am in a position to do is to say that this document was obtained by the Office of the Prosecutor from the Bosnian authorities some years back. You will see from examining the document that it appears to contain copies of receipts and various diagnoses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: -- and certificates, and of course it has to be taken -- obviously the panel will have to assess its value. Perhaps I could turn to the first relevant document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Trial Chamber has deliberated and feels that you are entitled to continue putting your questions, and we shall assess the medical data. We wish you to focus on the medical data because there are stamps and names and signatures here. Without this adversely effecting the work of the Prosecution, the Bench feels that your questions should focus on the medical data, with all due respect for the work you're doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And that was my intent, Your Honour, and I hope I won't be too long with this continuing aspect of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Mr. Cerenic, there's a lot of documents in this. If I could draw to your attention on the B/C/S version. At the bottom of the page you will see a long number starting 0031. If you could turn to 00315983, and it's page 6 on the English version. You told us that while you were in custody or while you were in detention on this first day that you were struck in the chest by this HVO soldier and that you sustained other injuries. Now, we have before us what appears to be a medical document making reference to a diagnosis for a contusion to the head. Status, cause, contusium capitus. Did you have injuries at the time to your head? And did you receive treatment from doctors after you were released from detention for these injuries?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Well, I said that I was hit all over. Now, as far as the head is concerned, that's true, and that's what I stated in what I said, that I had fractures on my head. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the Court's permission I have to use some time, but I have to say that this document does not have much value.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic. Mr. Kovacic, you know that what you say is of great interest to me. Let me get back to what happened last week. Everything occurred because you objected to the fact that the Prosecution was putting questions or the way the Prosecution was putting questions, and therefore the Trial Chamber had to intervene. We have already told you that you may raise objections. You may put your questions as part of the cross-examination. During the cross-examination you can turn to the -- to the witness and say, This document has no stamp, no signature, what do you feel about it? And then otherwise the Prosecutor will tell us that we are hindering their work. If you raise objections all the time to what the Prosecution is saying we will find ourselves in the same position as last week. The Bench has understood. We can see these documents -- well, the first page we don't know where it comes from. Also I realise and I can tell you now that undoubtedly some of the documents have undoubtedly been photocopied one on top of each other, the 315984. These are photocopies. Trust the Bench. We are perfectly capable of establishing the distinction here. I know whether the document is reliable or not, and you can trust me. That is for sure. I have all the time in the world. We can spend hours at this if you so wish, but is this in the interest of all the parties concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would agree as whole, but starting out from this struggle for time, I don't think there's any sense in losing time over a document that you probably will not admit into evidence tomorrow and then perhaps one of the parties will object, and then this will need greater time to solve the issue. But I just want to take the example of this document, and I won't go into the other medical documents. Based on this document and the date, it seems to have been compiled on the 15th of May, 1994. So that would be seven months later. Now, in the diagnosis we can see "post-contusion capo capitus." We all know that much Latin and we know what post-contusio capitus means. So from the witness statement these -- that's what he was suffering from, but contusio capitus, we all know that much forensic medicine. You can see that 10, 15, 20 days or a month after the injury, but seven months later there are no visible medical traces of contusio capitus, and then the physician goes on to say that the person suffered trauma. Yes, I do believe he did, but you can't see this from this piece of paper, this medical document, so it is just my proposal to save a minute or two, although I've spent five now, but to save future time because this is senseless. There is to sense to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I haven't been wasting the time. I was merely going to show the documents and it'd be a matter for the court to assess them afterwards, and if you have an objection you can file a written objection, and more power to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: So I was asking you, did you sustain injuries to your head?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And did you obtain treatment for those injuries?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Well, not adequate treatment. I did undergo examinations, but as to adequate treatment, not really, because I'm still -- well, I haven't got the money for the proper kind of treatment that I would need. I can't do that even today. As to my headaches, well, I have headaches and backaches and neck aches.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And if you look at the next document and the one after that, this makes reference to bruising to the chest. Did you sustain bruising to your chest, and did you receive medical treatment for that?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. That related to what I've already mentioned, the fractures, fractured ribs and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: That's all I wanted to ask you in that respect. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Are you leaving these -- these documents, Mr. Flynn?

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I just wanted to go to one last one, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: The document that we discussed initially, the one about the head, my colleague was suggesting that this was in 1994. When did you actually take treatment for that?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Would you repeat that question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: When did you actually take treatment for the bruising to your head? What period of time?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Well, as soon as I left. Well, not literally as soon as I left, but a couple of days later when the medical centre in Vares began functioning properly. I was supposed to go there and have some examinations in Zenica as well, because in Vares they didn't have the necessary equipment at the medical centre. But as I said a moment ago, I still haven't completed my treatment with respect to my head and cervical spine.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And the documents which we have now before us show that -- the dates and the certificates certainly on the English version show that the doctors looked at you and gave their opinions on -- inter alia between the 15th of December, 1994, and the 19th of January 1994. Would this be correct? Did you go to see the doctors during this period?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: When did you manage to go back to work?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: I didn't go back to the BH army for health reasons, as I said. Now, I can't quite remember when I began in 1994, but I did begin working in 1994, and the lady president of the War Presidency in Vares municipality persuaded me to start working, and I started working as an economist in Vares municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I don't have any more questions in relation to those. Perhaps before I move on to the next thing, Your Honour has something to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to ask you, Witness, have you seen any of these medical documents before? Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. They're my documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You have obtained them personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right, personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: If I need to say this, I can tell you that I have the originals at home. I have them stored at home, all of these.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Just as a follow --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Flynn, I do my job as a Judge here, but document 315983 - and I favour neither party - this document, I believe, is the document which concerns him. I do my job in all impartiality. I see that in the B/C/S version, I see a stamp which is half hidden. So an average Judge or a specialist will ask himself or herself whether this document is not a photocopy of two documents. Do you understand my point? I see this document, and I ask myself the question, and I can put the question to the witness. Witness, did you follow what I just said? Are you quite sure that this is a document --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I explain that? I'm sure that it is one document, and I can explain how this came about or how you happen to see this on two or three pieces of paper where you can see two stamps. Do you wish me to explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, yes, please. That's a question we have.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you can see, this -- these are smaller pieces of paper, and I put these little pieces of paper on one copy when I photocopied it. I put several of them on the photocopy machine so that I could copy them at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the truth of it, the whole truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Is it -- is it correct, Witness, that the document underneath is the document here on page 00315980? Because if one looks at what one sees at the bottom for the other documents, it always seems to be exactly what one sees on the document of the ophthalmologist, the doctor that examined your eyesight.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's precisely what I wanted to tell you. If you see if you look at the bottom they're the findings that come before the other documents, and they're the same ones --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Flynn.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Just as a follow on to Your Honours' questions:

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Do you remember whom you gave these documents to initially? Did you hand these documents over to the OTP, or did you hand them over to investigators from the BiH authorities? Do you remember? Did you hand the documents to anybody in authority?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: I think I gave them to the OTP. Already photocopied, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And you had performed the photocopies; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: I think I handed over the photocopy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Murphy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: -- to the extent it matters, and I don't know whether it does, if Your Honours are concerned with this, clearly it would be possible, from what the witness says, to have the original documents produced. I do notice some interest back on pages 54 and 55 of the transcript where Mr. Kovacic raised a point about the authenticity of the accompanying documents. Mr. Flynn represented that these documents, or that one, had been obtained from the Bosnian authorities, but now it now appears that it may have been obtained directly from the witness. So perhaps that can be clarified. And if the witness has the originals, it may be perhaps possible to have them faxed or -- so we can get to the bottom of the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I will undertake to -- to clarify it as much as I can for Your Honours. Our case manager tells me that the records at this point in time suggest that the document was obtained in 1995 from the BiH Ministry of Interior through the state security services in Visoko. It was in a file of events relating to Vares, dated the 23rd of October, 1993. I can't tell you any more, though, other than that at this point in time. I'll try and clarify it further for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Mr. Cerenic, just moving on, following your -- your ordeal in detention, did you form -- with others, did you form an association of ex-prisoners, of people who had been held in the detention centres?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And were you an official of that association?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: From the very inception, well I was the president of the association.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And can you tell Your Honours what -- very briefly what the purpose of the association, forming the association was for?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Well, the situation in Bosnia was such that as for organised groups, associations of citizens and things like that, attempts are made, well, to help people who got out of the war as invalids, veterans, then there are associations of camp inmates. An effort is made to help them exercise their rights, like the right to health insurance, medical insurance.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did you compile a list of those persons who had been held in the detention centres in Vares starting on the 23rd of October, 1993, up to the release that you described?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And what criteria did you use to compile that list? Did you refer to official documentation?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: The documentation that is required to prove that a person was a camp inmate are cards issued by the International Red Cross that are received on the spot. So that was one of the criteria for proving that somebody was a camp inmate.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, I'd ask you to turn to Exhibit 08850, and if you go to the last page. This appears to be a list of names compiled by the Association of Detainees from Vares, and on the last page there is a stamp and a signature. Do you recognise that signature on the B/C/S version?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's my signature. Yes, that's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And this list of names, there is a total of 249 names on it. Is this correct? Were there 249 people held in detention in Vares during the period which I referred?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: The figure is actual little bigger than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And for each of those persons that are on this list, did you have a corresponding ICRC document?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: I don't think that everyone had a document like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: How accurate is the list therefore?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: The list is 100 per cent accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, during the course of your evidence you told about being beaten, and you told about other people being beaten. Can I ask you to turn to Exhibit - I'll just get the number - 6180. Do you have it? This is a report dated the 28th of October, 1993.

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Issued by the Medical Corps of the HVO, of the Croatian Defence Council, and it's signed by Dr. Drazen Grgic. Did you know who -- do you know -- did you know Dr. Drazen Grgic?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Grbic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did you know Dr. Drazen Grgic?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Was he a medical officer assigned to the Croatian Defence Council in Vares?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Probably, because I saw him in uniform with HVO insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And did you see him -- did you see him in any of -- sorry, Mr. Kovacic is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that we have a mistake in the transcript, or my colleague misspoke. I'm not sure. On page 67, line 1, it says that the 28th of October is the date of this document. However, the date I see on the document itself is the 27th. So let's prevent any problems in terms of identification later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I was looking at the -- the -- and I see it on the Bosnian version too. 28th of the 10th, 1993, a daily report from the Bobovac Brigade for the 27th and the 28th of October, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid that we're not talking about the same document then if we are talking about 6180, and that is the one that appears on the transcript, too, 6180, that is a document issued on the 27th of October. That's what it says on the top of the page. And in the first line of the text, it says that it's a daily report of the Medical Corps of the Bobovac Brigade for the day of the 26th of October. So that is the identification of the document as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: You're perfectly correct, and my apologies. I was looking at the next document, which is --

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: So in this -- in this Exhibit 6180, you have a letter from the Medical Corps Bobovac Brigade dated the 27th of October, 1993, and if you look at the last sentence, it says: "There are 25 -- there are 251 Muslim civilians under supervision in two schools of which 27 sick and elderly people will be released today," and it's signed by Dr. Drazen Grgic. I think you've confirmed that he was the medical officer. Did you see him in either the high school or the elementary school at any stage while you were held there?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: I remember while we were at the Ivan Goran Kovacic secondary school, I remember that once he came in, in order to help us, those of us who were there. I don't know, to give us pills and dress our wounds. And then the HVO soldiers literally kicked him out of the room. I cannot remember his exact -- their exact words, but they were saying things like, "He's treating the balijas," or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And so Dr. Grgic would have been in a position to have seen the number of people in the schools; correct?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. Yes, he had been in a position to do that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And I think that the numbers you gave us originally exceeded 251. So when Dr. Grgic talks about 251 Muslim civilians, this is more or less in line with the numbers you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were several of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And would Dr. Grgic have been in a position to observe that people held there were beaten?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, a few minutes ago I said that he came with that intention, to help us. I'm talking about medical examinations, helping us that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: So if you turn to the next exhibit, two -- 6201 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Flynn, you're not referring to this document any more, 6180; right? You've finished with that document?

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: No. I now turn to 6201.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now, I'd like to draw your attention that when I compare the B/C/S version and the English version, since there seem to be a lot of translation problems here, we have to be very careful if the document is admitted. When I look at the it English version it indicates there were no report on Croatian civilians who were wounded and that the commander of the brigade informed the Medical Corps that there were 25 members of the MOS, Muslim armed forces, and then there's a dash and says 20 civilians who were killed in the battle of Stupni Do, whereas in the B/C/S version the text it says the word "I," - I - appears. And so my question is this, and I'd like to ask you this as well, Mr. Flynn. These 25 members of the MOS and 20 civilians, which would make it 45 persons killed. I'm not sure I understand the text as it stands.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Well, I'm not in a position to help you on that aspect, Your Honour, because this document is not produced with reference to this specific section of the document. The document is being produced purely by reference to the last sentence which -- which confirms that there were Muslim civilians under supervision in two schools. So I didn't examine the issue of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, very well, but there, Mr. Scott -- no, Mr. Scott. I was thinking of Mr. Scott, but I mean Mr. Flynn. You just said that your question was based on the last sentence, but when we, the Judges, have to deliberate in a number or in the coming years, I don't know what -- we're going to take a look at the document, which might be admitted, I don't know yet at this stage, makes mention before the 251 Muslim civilians that there were 25 members of the MOS and 20 civilians who were killed. So that's where my question's coming from.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: But my point is this, Your Honour, and it goes to what Mr. -- Mr. Scott was saying today, there are some questions we know we don't ask because we know the witness can't answer it. The witness wasn't asked to deal with this issue, because we know that he's not in a position to deal -- to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I can only address the last part of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. So that is quite precise. But what I'm saying is that, if we don't -- nobody comes back to that later on at a later stage, neither you or the Defence, the Judges, when they come to deliberate, are going to look at the document and they could reach certain conclusions on the basis of that. So that's what I want you to understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And it could well be the case that there may be another witness that will come before Your Honours at some stage during this crime base that will be able to address that issue, but certainly not this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I know that it's time for a break, but I'm almost finished. I don't know whether you wish me to continue or whether you ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just finish your question and we'll have the break afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: So I was asking you if you would move on to the next document, 6201. And you told us that Dr. Grgic would have been in a position to see detainees had been beaten --

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the witness did not really say that. He clearly cannot say what Dr. Grgic saw, and it's not an appropriate use of this document to try and prove it by those means. May we just point out how right Your Honour was in his separate opinion the other day to say that the Prosecution should call these witnesses in the right order, in which case these problems would not arise.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I'm going to ask the witness the question anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Mr. Cerenic, can you tell the panel whether or not Dr. Grgic was in a position when he came into the hall to see whether or not the prisoners had been beaten?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I don't know how he can answer that. I don't mind him asking whether he saw Dr. Grgic examining prisoners or looking around him and he can describe what the doctor would have seen if he was there at the same time, but how can he possibly as what conclusion Dr. Grgic should have drawn from that, which is exactly what he is trying to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: My response to that was the witness's evidence was he was beaten. There were a number of other people beaten. When he came in, he saw somebody beaten without it being drawn to his attention, and it's quite simple. Either he -- either the doctor, because of the conditions that prevailed in the hall, the doctor may have been in a position to see that there were people beaten. He may not have been in a position to see. I don't know. Perhaps we should let the witness answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, he could see. As a matter of fact, he tried to do something to some of them in medical terms. I don't know what it was; perhaps he wiped off the blood off their faces. And he went through the entire hall. He saw all of us. He could see us quite well. Of course he could see that people had been beaten up, of course. And he helped some of them, as I already mentioned, a few of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: So if you look at paragraph 4 of the letter of -- the gentleman is talking about 27 October 1993, Dr. Grgic says on the second sentence of paragraph 4: "Those detained have access to medical care and are allowed visits by UNPROFOR members unlike -- and unlike before, they are no longer beaten." Does this correspond to what you've just told us, that he would have been in a position to see that prisoners had been beaten?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Flynn, it looks as if you were done with this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Could I then add a question? Witness, can you confirm or deny that after the 28th of the -- of October, the prisoners were no longer beaten? That's what the doctor states in the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whether they beat the ones in the hall of the elementary school or secondary school, I don't know that. I already told you that I was at this third location. I was at Majdan. I think I was then at Majdan. It's already been mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I don't think I have any further questions for the witness, Your Honours. I'm sure Your Honours may have some questions, but I don't have any further questions at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Flynn. We shall have a break now, it's 25 to, and resume in 20 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: --- Upon resuming at 5.55 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. We have one hour and five minutes ahead of us. Mr. Flynn. MR. FLYNN: Just before you start with the cross-examination, Your Honours, I wonder, could Your Honours give me direction on the next witness. As you know, we had another witness scheduled for today, but given the lateness of the day, I'm interested to know whether your -- it will be Your Honours' intention. Perhaps my colleagues on the Defence could give you some indication whether they have many questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that would depend on the Defence teams, if their Defence has no questions to put. I don't know. We said that Defence counsel would have an hour and a half, so that would be 15 minutes for each Defence counsel. As far as I'm concerned, I can't tell you. This will depend on Defence counsel and the accused. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President and Your Honours. We'd like to thank the gentleman for coming here to give his evidence. We have no questions for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Murphy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: We don't have any questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that we were the first to be asked and we give our time to Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. Praljak asked to put a few questions to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic also?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that about 15 minutes. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] I actually tried to signal that we have some questions, but not more than 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So we shall begin. Who would like to start first? My colleagues are telling me that we won't have enough time, so I think it's better to ask the second witness to come tomorrow. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll do that, Your Honour. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Cross-examination by the Accused Praljak:

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness. I will have a few questions for you, so could you please tell me what you know, and what you don't know, just say that you don't know about it. I'm not going to deal with the bad things that happened to you. I don't really want to do that. I don't want to put salt into the wound, as it were, but we are going to deal with other matters. You said that Vares was surrounded by forces of the army of Republika Srpska on one side. You said Chetniks, but let's say the forces of Republika Srpska. And on the other side, the 2nd and 3rd Corps. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please put the microphone in front of you. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: You said that the HVO in Vares had some kind of agreement so that the convoy with food and other supplies would go through the area controlled by the army of Republika Srpska so that people could live there and have enough food.

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Do you know that this same corridor was used for the passage of the convoys that then went to Tuzla, for instance, via Vares?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Oh, you don't know about that. But you know that Tuzla was a big area with lots of people and that they had to eat something.

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Do you know of any other way in which convoys reached Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: You don't. Do you know that the population, the Croatian population from Kakanj left Kakanj or was, rather, expelled from Kakanj in June 1993?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Tell me, do you know who did that, who told them, "Go"?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: In their view it was done by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Do you know that more specifically this was done by the forces of the 3rd Corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Since Kakanj was within the then 3rd Corps, I guess that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, you're a metalworker by training.

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: In Vares -- well, Vares was a type of industrial centre, a smallish one, but a significant segment of the labour force was there.

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: That was one of the biggest mining towns in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: But what kind?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. Sorry, let me just say this: We exploited iron ore, whereas they had coal mines.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: All right. At the same time in Kakanj and in the surrounding villages there was a Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: In Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: No, sorry, Vares.

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And there was a relatively decent number of Serbs? Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Yes. Can I just add something to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Of course you can.

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: There were Serbs, some Serbs, and then they packed up and left Vares. So in this period that is essential to all of this, there were very few in Vares. That is to say in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: The year of 1993 is a long time.

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Well, October 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: But up until October there were Serbs there?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Well, then I have to say something. When the HVO forces attacked the Serb villages, Planinica and Slavin, now, when was this in what month, I can't remember exactly, I just know it was before the month of October. And I think that it was in summertime.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: So at that time the HVO was still fighting against the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Well, you know what? It wasn't actually fighting. It's not fighting like fighting that took place in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Well, I'm telling you now about what I heard. The HVO asked for the disarmament of these two villages, and since they refused to do that then they attacked them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: All right. At any rate, a military action to secure the rear area of the Serb villages. Can we put it that way?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: I'm not very competent to speak in strategic terms, whether that is the rear area or whatever. I just know that there was fighting, that there were casualties, that there were people wounded, killed. I don't know about the reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Well, so it's exactly the way I put it. There was fighting. But then let us go on. So these colleagues of yours, or parts that are called people who live in Bosnia, and your colleagues, workers from Kakanj, when they came, when they were expelled, as we say, what about the Bosnian Muslims and you personally? Did anybody go and see these people, talk to them, help them, try to explain what it was that happened, pacify them? There were thousands coming; right?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were lots of them coming. I think that the figure was about 15.000 or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Well, here comes a question. Do you remember that any of the SDA leaders, the Presidency that was in this village then, went to these people and said, "People, we're not the ones to be blamed for this"? Did they talk to them? Do you remember any such thing?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: I cannot really answer that with any degree of certitude. I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you. And do you know, for instance, that Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, who was the commander of all the forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that he issued some kind of order to all his forces saying, "What you did is impermissible, and you are going to return all the expelled people from Kakanj to their homes"? Are you aware of any such order?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: All right. Do you know in this area that was under the control of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- well, this is my question: At one point in time you went to this village, the name of which is -- just a minute, please. Davrani --

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Dabravine.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Dabravine. You went there, and at one moment you got a bit of rest and you went to Vares before all of these things that happened; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Do you know of any person from Kakanj going from Vares to Kakanj and asking for permission to cut some firewood there to provide heating for his family and things like that?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know about any such thing but they probably didn't want to do that. They probably didn't want to go. Because you have to take into account the fact that there were quite a few Croats, Catholics, in the municipality of Kakanj who stayed behind, who didn't go anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Well, what is this figure, if you know?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: I don't know, but I just know that there were quite a few of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Were they under the protection of the United Nations force there or were they free to move about Kakanj as they pleased?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: I think I would take up a lot of your time if I were to tell you by way of an answer all the things that I heard and all the things that I saw in terms of the Croatian population in Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: All right. What about people from Vares, Croats, either those who came from Kakanj or from Vares? Could they freely go to Zenica or Tuzla, for instance, to the free territory that was held by the two still regular armies of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HVO, that is?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Sorry, could you please repeat that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Well, Vares is full of people from Kakanj and is surrounded by people from the army of Republika Srpska and in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Tuzla and Zenica are under the control of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Do you know that these people in the free territory it of Bosnia-Herzegovina could freely go from Vares to Tuzla for medical treatment, to visit -- I'm talking about Croats, that is, to Tuzla or Zenica. Could they go freely?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Well, they could go to Zenica because there was a hospital there, the cantonal hospital, and Croats and Bosniaks and Serbs went there for medical treatment. I mentioned a while ago that Vares, for instance -- well, as far as medical services are concerned there aren't really that many. I don't know really about this medical terminology so I cannot express myself, but I think there is only electrocardiograms and X-rays. If they needed anything else they had to go to Zenica. Well, Tuzla is pretty far away from Vares. I don't know. I think it's over a hundred kilometres. I think it's over a hundred kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, please, do you know at the time all this was happening in Vares how many Croats were left in Zenica, and if there were few of them, where did they end up, those who had to leave Zenica?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: To tell you the truth I don't know, but I know as a member the army I heard from an elderly neighbour of mine who had some relatives in Zenica that he sent them things from Vares to Zenica or, rather, that I took things to these relatives of his. I don't know, like a sack of flour, oil, things like that. It's not that this Croat did dare not leave Vares, but simply that he was an elderly man and that's why. So that's the answer. There were more Croats who lived there in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: So you don't know the number of persons who remained or those who were expelled?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: No, I don't. You mean who was expelled from Zenica?

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: I don't know. As a matter of fact, I don't know whether anybody was expelled at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Fine. Now, tell me this, please: In your statement here you said that on the 21st or 22nd of October, 1993, 200 Ustasha soldiers turned up, Apostolis and so on. You used the word "Ustasha," right?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: So tell me, what are the Ustashas?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Well the term "Ustasha" is a term known from World War II and before, and I think that individual people in Vares felt this as something -- well, they liked being called Ustashas.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes. I don't question that.

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: But you know that at the time in Bosnia they were divided into balija, Ustashas, and Chetniks, the people, based on the ethnic composition, ethnic structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I know that certain people did use those terms, those expressions, but I don't know whether that should have been the case, whether those terms should have been used, but what I am asking you is the following: The Ustashas were an army of a regime in Croatia which together was linked to Germany, Nazi Germany, and they were convicted of crimes, and Ustashas were part of the army of that regime. You know that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, do you know the percentage of the armed forces of Croatia from World War II belonged to the Ustashas and to the Home Guards, the Domobrani or regular army?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Do you know how many Muslims in World War II were in the Ustasha units, members of the Ustasha units?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: I don't know that either. I can't tell you what the percentage is or the number is.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: All right. You never heard about the famous Handzar Division?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: It was an Ustasha division or, rather, a division that belonged to the Wehrmacht, the SS troops, that was predominantly composed of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: As I said, I have heard of the Handzar Division, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: All right. Fine. You went on to say the following, that the Croats took over the power and authority in Vares and, in a way, replaced the really elected authorities that moved to this village called Dabravine. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, in this legally elected government of the first democratic elections there was the had HDZ, the SDA, the communists or reformed communists, and the SDP and the Reformist Party of Ante Markovic. Were those the main parties in Vares?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's right. There were all these parties, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, when you went to Dabravine, was anybody in that legal authority, as you call it, from the SDB which was composed mostly of Serbs and partially of Croats as well? Can you remember a name from that legally elected authority in the first elections in the SDP and the Reformists with a Serb or Croat in that authority in Dabravine?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: I say with full responsibility that there were Croats in Dabravine as well, and in the War Presidency of the time in Vares municipality as well. For example, I'll give you a name. There was Kreso Romic, and in the War Presidency -- that was in the War Presidency under military structures too. Perhaps I'll omit to say somebody, but I know there was Kreso Romic, I know there was Ljudevit Mijatovic. There was Kreso Romic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes. Kreso Romic you've said twice.

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: I apologise if I said Kreso Romic twice. I know he was in the army so I tried looking at the civilian structure first but I think I gave three names. But there were more as regular soldiers, ordinary soldiers, and the legally elected government, authority for the entire population of Vares. It was the legal authority elected at the democratic elections with the proviso that at first I think those who won -- are you interested in that?

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Well, I know about that and I'll ask you my questions. Now, in the first democratic elections the SDP secured 26 or 7 seats - a witness told us that - of a possible number of 50 seats. Now, how many of those 26 SDPs were legally elected whether in this legal -- in this legal authority or government in Dabravine?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, tell me the following: When Vares, under the attacks of the 2nd and 3rd Corps when the Croats moved out, and when the authorities returned, you said, from Dabravine you're talking about a war Presidency. Now, who appointed the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: The War Presidency. Well, at the time I wasn't abreast of political trends, but who could have appointed the War Presidency at the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Why don't you say, I don't know?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: All right, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, tell me the following: Wouldn't it be logical once the authorities returned to Vares and it wasn't -- no longer the illegal government but the legal government, the legal authorities, and that people should have been returned from the results of the election of the 1990s who were legally elect. So those same people, to have them returned, without any need for a War Presidency at all, because the War Presidency means somebody imposing power.

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: No. All the Presidencies, the municipal Presidencies were referred to and called War Presidencies in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: All right. That's on the Bosniak side. Now, in that War Presidency did you have the same composition of people who were elected at the first democratic elections in Vares? That's what I'm asking you about. If you don't know, say so.

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat that question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: In the War Presidency, did you have the same people sitting in the War Presidency as were elected at the first democratic elections in Vares, the 13 HDZ members, 20 others, and so on, that kind of structure?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Right. You don't know. Now, do you know that in -- the expulsion of Croats from Kakanj, that the Mujahedin took part, too, who were in Zenica at the time?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Do you know anything at all about the number of Muslims who on the territory of Zenica existed -- well, the number of Mujahedin, I mean. Did you hear anything about the Mujahedin? Did you know anything about them, how many of them there were, the way in which they waged war?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: No, I knew nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Right, nothing. Tell me the following, please: After you went through all these terrible times, and I don't want to say anything nice about those terrible calvaries, that you had to experience, but when you went back to Vares with the UNPROFOR vehicles, did you come across Croats who had been there beforehand?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the elementary school there were Croats and Bosniak Muslims who found refuge or asked for refuge and shelter from the -- who asked the UNPROFOR forces for that. There were Croats and Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: So can we say most of the Croats left Vares?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Well, that would take time. Well, yes, most people did, most of them did leave Vares.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, these Muslims who sought shelter in this elementary school, what were they seeking shelter from, and safety from, since the BH army was already there? What were they afraid of? Were they afraid of parts of the BH army forces who did what they did in an uncontrolled manner in Vares? Can we put it that way?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't put it that way. It was a very special moment. You didn't know who was there, whether there were HVO soldiers or whoever. The Bosniaks fled without knowing that the entire Croatian population was evacuated from town and that with them all their army units had left as well. And if I tell you the following fact, that the Croats forcibly expelled the Croatian population from Vares to evacuate even those who did not wish to leave Vares.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: All right. Now, on the 23rd, in the morning, you were arrested in a very unseemly way and taken to the school.

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And you said for nine or ten days you were incarcerated there in different places, actually; is that correct? That's what you said, I believe.

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: No. If I remember what I said, the Prosecutor asked me how long I'd spent in the schools, the three schools, and then I said I spent six days or five or six days in the secondary school called Ivan Goran Kovacic, and that I spent two days in the elementary school in Vares on the third floor, and that then they hid us after that and that we spent in Majdan in the mines -- well, I don't know how long, but 14 or 15 days all together. That's the time I was incarcerated for.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, tell me, when you were in detention, when you were incarcerated during that time and some HVO members were mistreating you and beating you even five times a day, how did you come to learn that the HVO soldiers forcibly expelled Croats from Vares municipality, forced them out of Vares municipality?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: A moment ago I mentioned that while we were in Majdan, in the mine - this was prior to the evacuation of the Croatian population from Majdan - that the HVO vehicles were passing by and that an HVO soldier used a megaphone to appeal to the population to evacuate.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: They can -- they said that the defence lines had been broken and that there was no more protection. So that's why they appealed to them to evacuate. So that's all you could have heard. Now, did you ever hear or see any forcible evacuation of the population? And when I say forcible, when one says forcible, one means with rifles. Did you ever witness that?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: No. I wasn't at a place where I could see that, but we heard all about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Well, we all heard lots of things after the war, and that's the general principle. One hears terrible things after a war. But tell me the following: You were shown two documents here. One was from the doctor. What was his name? One was dated the 27th, and the other was dated the 28th. Now, if, as you say, you were in these three different schools before you went to Majdan, if you were there for nine days, and a moment ago you said that you did not see what the doctor could have done, et cetera, but is it correct that on the 27th and the 28th of October, 1993, you were in a school, an elementary -- a secondary school and saw the doctor arrive?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: I was in the secondary school and saw the doctor arrive, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And as a member of the HVO, the Medical Corps of the HVO, he went there to help the people, to tend to their wounds and so on?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And then some HVO members kicked them with their legs, with their feet, and threw him out; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Tell me the following: When the people of Kakanj arrived in Vares, and nobody called them back, nobody issued orders to the forces that had expelled them to have them returned, with this War Presidency which was established in Vares, did it happen that the entire -- the whole of the War Presidency or part of the War Presidency, did they go and say, the Croats of Vares -- "You Croats of Vares, come back, return from Kiseljak to Vares. We guarantee your safety and security. We guarantee that we will take care of you. We guarantee that you can move around liberated territory"? Did that happen?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Well, I did hear a document was sent to Kiseljak, but you couldn't go to Kiseljak for security reasons. However, I did hear that a document was sent to the War Presidency -- or from the War Presidency appealing to the Croatian population to return to Vares. And I think that at the beginning of 1994 people began returning -- the Croats began returning of their own free will to Vares.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now tell me the following --

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: I don't think; I'm quite sure, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: All right. Now, tell me the following: Are you aware that anybody from the Bosnia-Herzegovina Presidency issued orders to the commanders of the 2nd and 3rd Corps that they should form some elite units, send them to Vares, send representatives from these units and the civilian authorities to the Croats to say, Come back. We guarantee your safety now? Was that possible? Was that possible at all in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: I don't think I understood you. I do apologise, but I wasn't following. Could you repeat that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes of course. We have some more time. I can do that. Now, do you know -- you were working, attached to the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Very well. But anyway, from the Bosnia-Herzegovina Presidency did anybody issue orders to the army, to the commanders of the 2nd and 3rd Corps to form certain units, send them into that area, and then tell the civilian authorities, "Go and call the people, appeal to the people who left this area to return because we guarantee their safety and security on the free territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina"? If you're not aware of that, then you don't know.

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Right. Now, tell me this: Do you know that whether to the Bosniaks in Vares the people of Kakanj, the Croats from Vares and the Serb inhabitants that were there, whether they from any part of the then authority in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Presidency, for instance, of Tuzla, Zenica, whatever, whether they received any material resources at all, fuel, weapons, firewood, food, anything like that, salaries?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Right. You don't know. Now, do you know, when you returned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you. I would only like to ask you how many more minutes would you like to take because of the other counsels as well. So let us -- because we now have 30 minutes left. Thank you. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. That was my last question, actually. I wanted to round off the questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, if these people in Vares gathered together in that way, were not able to leave freely to Zenica or Tuzla unless under some special agreement with the Serbs, they didn't receive flour or oil or anything like that, were they a sort of -- how shall I put it mildly? Was this a sort of closed camp, a closed environment which depended on some convoys coming in from Croatia and passing through Serb territory, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that a place like that, in an encirclement without having any resources coming in, probably [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: My last question is this: When you yourself returned to Vares, when you returned to Vares, you found the BH army in Vares. Do you know that the BH army, when it entered Vares, looted, set fire to the place? Did you see this on television, on any TV footage, or did you see it with your own eyes when you entered Vares? Did you see what Vares looked like after the BH army had entered? Give us a frank answer.

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
