utterances.text: That's what I want to tell you. I didn't go in after the army, but UNPROFOR broke -- brought us in when the town was empty of both armies, the HVO and the BH army. That's when we were brought there. And they took us to the elementary school, and we spent the night there or however much time, and I went home after that because my wife had already been evacuated by UNPROFOR to the UNPROFOR base. She returned -- or, rather, she had her key and she was able to unlock our front door. And later on, to answer your question whether I saw anything, I did not because I spent several months being -- I was very ill for several months, and I would just go to the health centre for treatment from my house in a car. I didn't move around town.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: But Vares is a small town --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, would you tell the Chamber how many last questions you intend to ask? Because you had before an answer it was the last one. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Well, yes. I just wanted to clarify this, what can be seen from the car when you go through a small town and what the situation was, especially since all of this was shown on television too. I wanted to ask him what he knew about what this town looked like after the liberation army of Bosnia-Herzegovina entered town.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Well, what I saw was that there was a building that had been torched by the HVO soldiers when they were leaving, and also I saw where the military police was, the HVO military police. At that place where they were, the windows were broken.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I just have to ask you one more thing. How did you see the HVO torch that building?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Because that was -- well, I don't know. I say that -- in that evacuation of the population it was set ablaze while the soldiers of the HVO were still in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: A moment ago you said that you entered town when the HVO was no longer in town. Thank you very much. No further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will have just a few very simple questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you first tell us whether you handed over all your medical documentation to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I don't know, but all the medical documentation from that period. Well, perhaps not all of it, but I have all the originals at home.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because if I saw this medical documentation well in the exhibit that was shown to you by my colleague from the Prosecution, it is obvious that the 31st of December, 1993, is the date of the first document, and now you told us that as soon as you came to Vares, that is to say on the 30th -- or, rather, on the 3rd of November, 1993, you went to see a doctor. So I was wondering how come there were no medical documents for these roughly one month and 20 days or so. Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how to explain this to you as simply as possible. I went to the health centre, but -- how should I put this? - I didn't get any findings or any major findings. Or I couldn't conduct any big-time tests there. First I went there and I just got some pain-killers, pills for, I don't know, headaches for the most part, and mostly for my ribcage. I mentioned already that I had fractured ribs, and they used some kind of medical bandages for treating that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The first document, your first document, actually, is a prescription for eye-glasses; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Witness, why did you use the words "Ustasha" as in Chetniks when you talked about members of the HVO and members of the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Well, I've already mentioned that once. That's terminology that was used for the three peoples.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What about the word "balija"? Is that something that is equal categorisation for the Muslim people too?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what they called us.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You've said to us that you testified before the cantonal court in Zenica about what happened in Stupni Do. Can you just tell it us what trial this was, against who?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: As for Stupni Do, I did not take part in that on account of what was going on in Stupni Do. Actually, these were proceedings against Dominik Iljasevic, Como.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell it us, was it quite customary for members of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, all the way up to September 1993, come home to get only rest, to spend a few days in Vares, and then return to their respective units?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. Yes, it was it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did you come to Vares in your military uniform or in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: No, in civilian clothes. Would you like to hear why it was that people came?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Perhaps later if we have enough time. You told us that Vares is a small town, as you had put it.

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, the inhabitants of Vares, did they know that you were a member of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina? I assumed that that was no secret. Was it?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Well, most people knew.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, the unit that you blocked to, you told us that this was the platoon attached to headquarters. Was this an independent platoon or was this a platoon within a larger military unit?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: It was the platoon attached to the headquarters or to the War Presidency of the municipality of Vares.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, the command of your platoon, was it aware of the plans of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in terms of Vares and the surrounding area?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What about you personally? Did you have any knowledge about the plans of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina to take Vares?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, in September 1993, when you came to Vares, was it approximately the end of the month, mid-September?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: I think it was the beginning of the month, the beginning of September.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When you say that you got a 30-day furlough; right?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Yes, a month.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, how was it that you were in Vares in -- on the 23rd of October? That's about 20 days longer than that.

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, I asked subsequently for some additional leave, because I had not prepared firewood. I explained that a few moments ago. I had to do this by hand so that I could provide for my family so that they would have something for the winter by way of firewood.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, as you lived in Vares did you hear that there, before the 20th of October, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina had taken some Croatian villages in the surrounding area of Vares?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What about the village of Kopljari? You didn't hear of that village falling into the hands of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: I'm telling you again that I was preoccupied with this work that I came to do so that I could go back to my job properly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You spent all your time in the woods cutting firewood?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, most of the time. If you do it by hand it takes a long time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. We all know how this is done.

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Yes. And the forest is pretty far away from my home.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: On the 23rd of October, you say that that's the day when you were brought into custody, tell me, were all the detainees men? All the persons brought into custody, were they men?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, were they military-aged men?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: All ages.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Military-aged men or not?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: There were all ages there. Military age, older ones, and then also younger boys of, say, 17 to 18, up to some kind of grandfathers, people who were about 70.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You know full well that military-aged men are boys age 16 or even 15 according to regulations of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: I don't know what it was at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, at that time among the members -- among the people who were there, in addition to yourself, were there any other members of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me how many?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Would it correspond to the group that you mentioned that was singled out specifically?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: No, no. There were perhaps a total of three or four of us, not more than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. You said to us today that you were not released but that you escaped.

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: From Majdan.

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us about this in greater detail, how it is that you managed to escape? And, with your permission, before that I would like to remind you of part of your statement, and I will tell you what the date was. The 7th of April, 1994, given to the centre for the investigation of war crimes. You then said in terms of how you left, you said the following: "A night before the army entered Vares --" that's the very end of the document that I'm quoting from. "The night before entering Vares, we had no guards so we were wondering how to escape. Around 9.00 the guards came and asked us what we needed. They gave us buckets to relieve ourselves, and water, but we were not given any food in that prison. Seeing the movements of Croats from Vares, we knew that our people would enter town soon. "The next morning we called the guards, but no one responded to us, and one of us always kept guard by the door to see whether anybody would come up and free us. After a while a truck was heard near the prison. We thought that it was the HVO army, and we were getting ready to defend ourselves. However, Kreso Pejcinovic came and told us that he was going to see Ivica Gavran to see what to do with us. However, if he would not come soon that we should run wherever we could."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note we did not have the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, what I read out to you, does it actually correspond to what happened before you left the facility where you were?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Yes. Do you want me to explain how this happened?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. No details. You gave a very similar statement later on as well. There is no need for me now to elaborate, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Flynn.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I apologise for -- for intervening. I think it would be only fair if Ms. Alaburic would read the next sentence to complete the paragraph, and the entire matter would fall into context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You're quite right, Mr. Flynn. It is always good to understand a sentence against a backdrop of the general context.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So the next sentence is: "An hour later, Meho Trklja broke the door. We went into the hall, and we let the others go till we went to the UN, and they transferred us to Vares to a safe place." I don't think that what follows changes the sense of what I read earlier on in any way. My intention was not to skip these two lines that are usually read.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So, Witness, does this correspond to what happened as you were leaving the facility where you were detained?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Yes, because the HVO soldiers that were guarding us left having told us that they would leave us on our own for a few hours to see what was going on with their families. So that is how we had no guards, and that's how all of this happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Just one more question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. Alaburic, would you be kind enough and tell the Chamber from which document you have been quoting.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a statement that we got from the OTP, a statement by this witness to the Centre for Investigating War Crimes on the 7th of April, 1994. This document was not exhibited by the Prosecutor, but I assume, Your Honours, that you have received all of the statements made by this witness just as we have. I can read the ERN number, too, if you wish. There is yet another statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: The exhibit number would be of use. I see Mr. Kovacic shaking his head. We do not have it, just for your information.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Trechsel, I've just said the Prosecutor did not exhibit this document.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may be of assistance to my colleague. Your Honours, of course we don't know what it is that you received or not, but in previous situations it seems that you always received these statements made by the witnesses involved to the Prosecutor and also statements given to the Centre for the Investigation of War Crimes, if any. So far this seems to be the case. We apologise. Of course, we don't know what the OTP gives to you and what they give to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do apologise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The fact is sometimes we have no statement at all. Sometimes we have a statement given to the investigators to the OTP. Sometimes we have more, but this time we have just one. I'm not blaming anybody. I just want you to know. But I also wonder whether you should not leave the floor to Ms. Tomasegovic Tomic who wanted, I think, 15 minutes. I don't know. Maybe you have direct contact between the two of you to make sure that no one gets frustrated by the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, absolutely. Well, my colleague tells me that she won't need more than five minutes. I simply have one more question left, and I've cut my questions as short as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, in your statement to the OTP you spoke about the changed atmosphere in Vares itself in September 1993 when you came for that 30-day leave. Can you tell us what this change in atmosphere was, since you haven't spoken about this until now?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Well, the attitude of the Croats from Vares - well, not all of them - had changed, at least among some of them. I repeat yet again, Vares is a small town. We all knew each other, and, as we say, people who were my friends until only yesterday no longer wanted to look at me. I don't know for what reason, but they simply didn't want to and --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Sorry. I need to put questions to you. This change of atmosphere, did it have anything to do with the arrival of 15.000 inhabitants of Kakanj in Vares?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Probably. The people from Kakanj were angry at the Bosniaks and the people of Vares.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm going to remind you of your own statement. Paragraph 4, for those who want to check. You say that it was hard to get into town because about 15.000 Bosnian Croat refugees from Kakanj had some to Vares, that they were angry with the Bosnian Muslim inhabitants of Vares since they blamed the Bosnian Muslims and the ABiH for having been expelled from their homes. Is that correct what I read out just now from your statement?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you still think so?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, these 15.000 Croats from Kakanj, where were they put up? Were any of them staying at the school?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: That's why they were angry at the Vares Croats, because they had to be put up there. Again I'm saying it's a large number of people who came in Vares. They were put up the elementary schools and -- well, in the building of the elementary school and the secondary school. I don't know what the name is of this particular facility now where there are some rooms sort of, and that is where they were put up. That is where there were some makeshift toilets above the river and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, were they schools and facilities in which you were put into, you and the Muslims of military-able age who were incarcerated on 23rd of October, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. They were two schools, the two Vares schools, but we were put in into the halls of the elementary school and secondary school, and they were placed in the classrooms that had already been adapted. Well, not adapted, but they had already been rearranged to take in these refugees. There were blankets there and mattresses and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And if we can use the word you inherited what was there?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: No. No. We in the hall didn't find anything there. There was nothing in the hall when we arrived. You know these gym mats -- do you know what a gym mat is?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do know what a gym mat is.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My time is up unfortunately so I have to stop and give my colleague a chance?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. Alaburic. Cross-examination by Ms. Tomasegovic Tomic:

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm on my feet as quickly as possible and my question follows on something you said from the direct examination, and then Judge Trechsel asked you something linked to that, and I think that once you answer my question you will have in part answered Judge Trechsel's question and what he had in mind when he asked, and as well as Mr. Praljak's question. Now, we heard today that on the 27th and 28th you saw that Dr. Grgic or, rather, you didn't know what his name was at the time, but you saw that on the basis of the document later on, that he was in the hall, in the school hall, and that he was giving medical assistance there and that he was even attacked physically; is that correct? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: The second part is correct but I didn't say nor do I claim now that was on the 27th or the 28th or any date. I didn't mention any date when I saw Dr. -- Drazen in the hall. I didn't mention any date nor did I know what the date was.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But you did see his arrival in the hall and the events that took place there.

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Then you said you were transferred to Majdan; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: From the is secondary school we were transferred to the elementary school and from the elementary school to Majdan.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And then you were guarded in Majdan by guards who were soldiers and military police belonging to the Bobovac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You said that they didn't physically abuse you in Majdan or beat you.

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: May we now take a look at a document together? You can look at it on your screen it is 5D 02017, the number of the document. You'll get a hard copy as well. You already have the hard copy, I believe. And it is a document dated the 28th of October, 1993, from the brigade commander, the Bobovac Brigade, Kresimir Bozic, sent to the military police of the HVO, and judging by what we saw of the documents today it would be on the second day of Dr. Grgic's visit. Now, may we have a look at the first sentence of this document, and it said: "I prohibit the application of repressive measures, and especially physical abuse and mistreatment of persons temporarily placed in isolation in the area of responsibility of the HVO Bobovac Brigade." Now, according to my calculations you came to Majdan after the 28th of October. If you were arrested on the 23rd, you spent five or six days then?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Probably we were at Majdan if I can do the sums properly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: According to my calculations from this document it would emerge that in Majdan, this act prohibiting physical mistreatment was put into effect. Is that right? We've already said that, actually. Just give me a yes or no answer.

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: Well, probably it did apply. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Flynn, do have any re-examination in the few minutes we left?

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I had just one question. I don't know if the witness can answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Mr. Cerenic, Mr. Praljak asked you in the course of his examination something about the Croatian population leaving Vares and you said the Croatian population was expelled and that those who did not wish to leave Vares even had to leave. They were forced out by their own people. You didn't see this, but you heard about it. Can you tell us who you heard about it from?

utterances.speaker: SALEM CERENIC
utterances.text: To be quite honest I can't remember the name of the person but he's there to the present day, and it's a story going round Vares and the Croats said so, too, when they came to Kiseljak as refugees that they were called "the balijas of Vares. We should have killed you, too, in Vares." So that was the story told to the present day in Vares, the rumour going round. But I can't recall who it was I heard it from first.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Okay. I don't have any further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I thank you for having come to testify about the events that took place in your country. I wish you a safe journey home. I shall ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm now turning to Mr. Mundis to ask him what has been planned for tomorrow. We are running late, because I understand there was a witness waiting today. I don't know, can we catch up on lost time, Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm certain we'll do everything we can to catch up. I'm meeting with members of the team tomorrow morning to see what further cuts can be made in order to get us through the remaining six witnesses that are scheduled. We will start tomorrow morning with the witness previously scheduled for this afternoon, so we will go in the same chronological order set as set forth on the calendar but we will be taking a look to see where time can be saved, if at all possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. If the witness is not a protected witness could you give thinks name, the one you intend to call tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I believe that protective measures either have been sought or will be sought with regard to the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We shall reconvene tomorrow. We will be sitting in the afternoon this morning -- this week, and we shall meet again tomorrow at a quarter past 2.00, which will give me enough time to read through the transcripts.
